Mr. Speaker, may I say a word on the point of order. I do so in particular because of the remark just made by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. Actually he has misquoted what the member for Skeena said yesterday, and the misquotation goes right to the pith and substance of one of the matters that is concerning us.
The hon. member for Skeena is fully aware of the citation in Beauchesne which says that questions must have some urgency. What he objects to, and what I object to, is the new twist that has been put upon this by Your Honour by saying that what is involved is the urgency of getting a reply. I submit with all respect to Your Honour that you have confused this with the wording that relates to standing order 26. In respect to standing order 26, relating to motions to adjourn the house to discuss matters of urgent public importance, there is wording in Beauchesne that says the urgency in that case means the urgency of having a debate. The point the hon. member for Skeena made yesterday was that nowhere in the citations in Beauchesne is there any wording that suggests that questions on orders of the day can be asked only if there is urgency in getting a reply.
It is our view that questions have to have some urgency, some immediacy, but that they cannot be denied because they are only urgent questions rather than questions concerning which it is urgent to get a reply. It seems to me that this is a fine distinction and it is something that does not exist in Beauchesne so far as questions on orders of the day are concerned. If I may say so with all respect, Your Honour is adding confusion to the situation by transposing into our practice with respect to orders of the day questions the phrase that appears with regard to motions under standing order 26. By the same token, I suggest that there is nothing in the citations in Beauchesne regarding orders of the day questions that denies the asking of questions merely because their answers are of a statistical nature.
I recognize, as the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka has just said, that the judgment as to whether or not a question is in order is in the hands of the Speaker. This puts a tremendous responsibility upon Your Honour. But I suggest that Your Honour has to have consideration not only for the practice

Inquiries of the Ministry of the last five years that some members can quote, but for the practice of the last 20 years that some of us can also quote. I feel that too many new twists, new interpretations, are being brought into the rules in respect of questions on orders of the day. I agree with the hon. member for Port Arthur, who pointed out last night that this should not develop into what it is fast becoming, a contest between members and the Chair. This orders of the day period is a time when members on the opposition side and the government side put questions to the ministers.
I recognize immediately that we have a responsibility. I deny the hon. member's statement that my colleague or I have asked questions we knew were out of order. I think every question I have asked has been a proper one to ask on orders of the day.
I submit there should be very serious consideration before new rules that are not in Beauchesne at all are carried into our practice regarding orders of the day questions.

I realize that there has been a change in the orders of the day question period as compared to previous occasions in this house. I do not wish to get involved in a piecemeal discussion at this time in that regard. In this context I would prefer to defer my explanation in regard to this matter until such a statement has been made, which I trust will be on either Monday or Tuesday. We have a great many questions on Monday, so I think I would prefer to defer it until Tuesday.
In so far as the reference by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is concerned, that this seems to have degenerated into a contest between hon. members and the Speaker, I say that is the last thing I wish it to be. I sometimes have felt, and I am not being facetious, that all the fast curves and the high, hard ones have not been confined to a certain contest that has been taking place in the United States and in which there has been a general interest by all hon. members. I feel it would be a rather poor situation should the Speaker have to sit as a sort of constable or policeman to police the conduct of hon. members; that would be the last thing on earth I would wish. The position of the Speaker is that of arbiter in this house, to observe the rules which are made by this house and which are binding on the Speaker.

In so far as the orderly conduct of business is concerned, I submit to the house that it is as much the responsibility of hon. members as it is of the Speaker. I bespeak their cooperation, and can assure them they will have the co-operation of the Chair.
In the light of what I have just said perhaps we could defer the point of order raised by the hon. member for Skeena until I have made a full declaration on the subject of questions during orders of the day.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The house in committee of the whole on a certain proposed resolution to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act. Shall the resolution carry?

Mr. Chairman, the Export
Credits Insurance Act at present provides a ceiling of $200 million for export credits insurance under section 14 which the corporation may underwrite at its own risk. There is also a ceiling of $200 million for export credits insurance under section 21 which the corporation may underwrite upon the authority of the governor in council, and the risk is for the government's account. Finally, there is a ceiling of $300 million under section 21 (a) for long term financing.
Under section 21, in cases where the board of directors of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation is of the opinion that a proposed contract of insurance would impose upon the corporation a liability for a term or an amount in excess of that which the corporation would normally undertake, and if in the opinion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce it is in the national interest that the proposed contract of insurance be entered into, the governor in council may authorize the corporation to issue the insurance policy.
Under section 21 insurance policies in force today and commitments given for sales under negotiation have reached the $200 million ceiling. There is substantial additional business in the offing; therefore in order to help exporters make the sales it is proposed that the present ceiling of $200 million be increased to $400 million.
Under section 21 (a) the government has authority, through the corporation, to finance export sales of capital goods. This financing is provided only in cases where credit terms extending beyond five years are required. These separate facilities for long term financing were made available little more than a year ago, and to date contracts totalling some $50 million have been signed. Commitments

Export Credits Insurance Act to provide for financing total $108 million. Thus $158 million out of the $300 million available has been committed.
While this long term financing is in the nature of export trade promotion, at the same time from the point of view of recipient countries it represents aid to their development programs. All other capital goods exporting countries which provide long term credits to developing countries get recognition for the aid they are providing in this manner. Thus Canada has a fund of $300 million which is being used for aid to the developing countries, and at the same time is of tremendous benefit to Canada's capital equipment manufacturers.
The purpose of the proposed amendment to section 21(a) is to enable the corporation to accept promissory notes direct from importers. The present act restricts the corporation (a) to guaranteeing an instrument- that is, a promissory note-given by an importer to an exporter and (b) to purchasing a guaranteed instrument. The proposed change would facilitate the negotiating of business and improve the administrative procedures.
Both export credits insurance and export credit financing are important features of our drive to get Canadian manufacturers into the export markets of the world. The government for its part is doing everything possible to encourage exporters. With these facilities in Canada we are offering Canadian exporters the equivalent of anything available to exporters in any other country.
The service provided by the Export Credits Insurance Act is available to every Canadian producer, no matter what kind of product he wishes to ship abroad; farm products, fishery products, industrial raw materials, manufactured goods, any kind of product. It is designed to help and encourage all Canadian producers to extend their operations into the export field, by taking the risk out of the export business; it guarantees payment to the exporter. The operations of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation cost the taxpayers of Canada nothing, as the premiums charged for the services rendered are set to just cover the cost of operation. They do not provide a profit for the corporation or the government.
This legislation, as it has operated since December, 1960, when the government decided to use section 21(a) to make long term financing facilities available to exporters, provides Canadians with a service which is equal to that supplied by any other country in the world, and superior to that provided by all but a very few.
This is the kind of measure that is good for Canada, as it enables all Canadian producers

to enlarge their operations, and by so doing reduce their costs and make their products more competitive. By making their products more competitive as against those from other countries, both in the Canadian market and abroad, our producers increase their sales and provide more jobs for Canadians.
The need for amending the act to increase its ability to serve Canadian producers is a good indication of how our export trade has been expanding during the past two years. It has been growing at a rate of approximately 10 per cent a year, and this measure is intended to help that growth continue.
The purpose of the act is to help Canadians help themselves to sell their products in all markets of the world, and thereby expand the country's economy and provide more jobs for our people. I hope all hon. members will approve of this measure, and will support its passage in the house. I also strongly urge them to advise the producers in their constituencies of the services made available to them by this act, so they may make use of those services and thereby enlarge their operations.

I thank the minister for the explanation which he has given of the resolution. The resolution seems to do two things. It asks the committee to pass on the expediency of increasing from $200 million to $400 million the limit of liability of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation under contracts of insurance entered into under section 21 of the act; it also asks for approval of the right to introduce a bill to provide for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act. I assume we shall have an opportunity to see those other administrative changes when the bill is presented to the house, and that there will be time to consider them before the measure comes up for second reading.
The history of this legislation appears to me to be good. I think the provisions which have been made for export credit have done a great deal to assist the development of trade in this country since the end of the war. It is interesting to note the changing problems which have faced exporters as the years have gone on. The problems facing exporters now are wholly different from those which existed when the act was brought into force in 1944. The administration of the act seems to have been good, and the measure has undoubtedly contributed much to the development of our export trade. I would think, therefore, having heard the minister's assurance that authority to expend additional funds is required, that there should be no objection on the part of the committee to this resolution.

Export Credits Insurance Act
There are some questions I should like to ask and some explanations I should like the minister to make in connection with the proposed increase. They are of a purely factual nature, but sometimes it is difficult to obtain the kind of information required in connection with a resolution of this sort. In his opening remarks the minister stated that the amount authorized under section 13 of the act, that is the authority of the corporation to insure, was $200 million. Section 14 of the act provides simply that the limit of the authority of the corporation to insure shall not at any time exceed a total of ten times the aggregate of the amount of the subscribed capital and the surplus of the corporation. The first question which arises is, what is the subscribed capital and what is the surplus of the corporation at the moment? The minister will recall that the word used in the act in section 14 is "surplus" and that the financial statement deals first with the capital surplus paid in by the Minister of Finance and then with the earned surplus. The issued capital is shown at the sum of $15 million and there two items of surplus, capital and earned, making a total of more than $20 million, and it is difficult to see how the hon. gentleman arrives at the figure of $200 million under that section. I have no doubt there is an explanation, and I shall be glad if the minister will give us this information when he replies, because I think it should be on record.
The latest financial statement is, of course, contained in the annual report up to December 31, 1961. If the minister will tell us what changes have taken place in the capital set up since then we would be most obliged.
Then under section 21 I understood the minister to say that commitments at the present time have reached the authorized limit of $200 million, or very close to it. I should like the minister to place on record a list of those contracts. Perhaps he wants to do it in a form which would give the nature of the contracts and not the individual transactions, but I think we should have it. Then under section 21(a) the amount committed, I take it from his remarks, is $158 million. The amount authorized under that section is $300 million, so I take it there is no need to increase the authority there.
I do note from his remarks that he is making some changes having to do with the dealing in paper, the guaranteed paper, and the promissory notes under section 21(a). That raises the question which I raised when the amendments to this act were before the house on another occasion, namely whether or not the operations under section 21(a) should be carried on under a separate corporation, because the operations under section 21(a) are
in fact operations in the nature of financing or discounting of paper with regard to exports. There was no strenuous argument in the house as to whether or not that should be done.
I should like the minister to advise the committee whether he has considered that matter further and, if so, what his views are about it. It may well be that it need not be done, but it is something which should be looked at; because the operations of section 21(a), while very beneficial and supplementary to those under sections 13 and 21, are of quite a different nature. It is a point of administration which should receive careful consideration and watching, so that if the experience in administering the act does indicate that the two functions should be separated and that the functions under section 21(a) should be given to a separate corporation, it will be done.
In asking for authority for an extra $200 million under section 21 the minister merely indicated that the present $200 million had been committed. He did not indicate the requirement for the additional $200 million, and I should like him to indicate as best he can what he expects that $200 million to be used for. There is a nice question here as to the amount which should be granted by way of increase which has not been dealt with by the minister, as I think I can show in a minute, and I am sure he will seek to deal with this point.
Another point that has always concerned me with regard to this legislation is that all our export credit transactions are not financed under this one piece of legislation. There was quite an argument in the house during the last parliament as to why the sale of wheat to China was not financed under the authority of this act, bearing in mind that all previous sales of wheat which had been made to communist countries were financed by credit under this act, and bearing in mind also that the act provides what seems to be the type of machinery required for financing that kind of transaction. I think it fair to say of the last house that hon. members generally approved the sale of wheat to China. I think there was no controversy on that point.
Oh, oh.
Well, the hon. member for Athabasca interjects, but may I remind him that he will find that exact remark in my previous speech on this measure.
I did not interject.

I am sorry; it was another hon. member. In any event, that is an exact quotation of what I said earlier on that very subject, so there can be no doubt about it.

Export Credits Insurance Act
I	think it is a fair statement to say that there was no opposition at all to the sale of wheat to China.
The question raised by me was as to the legality of the guarantee given by the government; because instead of giving it under this statute, where authority is clear, the government gave it under an order in council which does not make any direct reference to the authority for that order. When I placed a question on the order paper as to what was the authority for that order in council, I was given an answer which I must say was not a model of clarity; that is putting it very gently. In any event, it appeared from that answer to he claimed that the authority lay in section
II	of the wheat hoard act. Of course section 11 of the wheat board act, according to the best opinions I can find on the subject and certainly from my own reading of the section, and from anybody else's to whom I have shown the section, does not authorize any such guarantee at all.
The significance of that is this; that under the Export Credits Insurance Act, with which we are now dealing, the necessary orders in council are required to be tabled within a certain time limit, and an opportunity is given hon. members to find out the facts and deal with the matter. I want to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if the extra $200 million he is now asking is intended to be used to finance the further sales of wheat to China, or what are his intentions as to the use to be made of this sum.
I for one take exception to the method used for the guarantee on the large wheat sale to China. I think it withheld from the house the right to know about and to discuss a matter that is of prime concern, and which must remain the responsibility of the house, namely the expenditure or commitment of public funds or taxpayers' money, however worthy and beneficial to the community at large. I have always been mystified as to why the government did not adopt the proper method of bringing that transaction before the House of Commons, either by bringing it under this act or, of course, by means of an item in the estimates, as can be done. Therefore I hope the minister will deal with that point.
The minister also made a general reference in his remarks to the increase in export trade. The feature about that which alarms many hon. members is that a very large proportion of that increase in export trade, at least on the figures available for last year, represents sales on credit to communist countries. That raises a difficult question, but one that it is a mistake to brush aside, and it should be faced. I hope our export figures will go up

sharply, but it would be a foolish person indeed who did not recognize that there are very great problems facing our exporters.
I am critical of the government for not taking other appropriate measures to increase our export trade. The government have brought in amendments to this measure from year to year as required. They seem to use this act, as far as I am concerned, rather well in relation to the needs of the exporters; but with regard to other more important matters of policy in relation to other governments or to other countries, in my view they have been either mishandled or neglected. I hope that in granting approval of this resolution for this increased authority under the Export Credits Insurance Act, we are not to be interpreted as in any way acquiescing in or condoning what I regard as the scandalous mishandling of our international trade negotiations.
I have reference to what I regard as the wholly wrong method of handling of the common market problem, starting off with the action of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance with their speech at Ghana, which speech incidentally was not released to the House of Commons although it was released to the press. It seemed to be a rather strange way of doing things. In any event, when we obtained the text from the press we found that it showed a shocking lack of understanding of the nature of the developing trade problems of the world and the appropriate methods by which to meet them.
I do not intend to redebate the matter now, but anyone concerned with the development of export trade must indeed have been greatly troubled by the negative and destructive approach of the Prime Minister at the recent meeting in London, where his whole approach to the problem was to prevent a healthy development of export trade and to fail to seek in that relationship and in that context to develop our trade. Then again there is to be considered the failure of the government to appreciate the tremendous changes in trade policy that have come about in the United States in the last few months, more particularly in their relationship to the common market. It seems to me that we should have immediately taken steps to come into proper relationship with those changes so that when the negotiations are carried on with the common market it will be our industry and our producers who will have the opportunity of participating in any advantageous agreement that can be made and not merely an agreement for the benefit of the particular industries and producers of the United States, with our benefit being merely

to the extent that we produce the same things or have the same industries. It seems to me that in that matter there was on the part of the government a failure that is not helpful in increasing our exports.
Then, of course, there is to be taken into consideration the whole unfortunate attitude with regard to trade with Cuba. As far as I am concerned it has always been a reflection on the present government. I cannot put the matter any more directly than that.
Tell us your idea.

The hon. member raises that question. We start right off with some of the nonsensical remarks of the minister, one of which was that you cannot do business with any better businessmen anywhere in the world than the Cubans. I think you just do not handle a difficult subject in that way in apparent conflict with our neighbour to the south with whom we do a greater volume of trade, by a very large margin, than any other country in the world. When they are adopting one policy we do not carelessly go about acquiescing in what may amount to back door methods of defeating their policy. I believe the government has become a bit more watchful following some episodes early in the year and at the end of last year, and 1 am appreciative of this fact. To that extent I give them credit. However, that is a difficult situation. I think the government's handling of it has been clumsy to say the least.
There is one other aspect of this matter of export trade that I should like to mention. This measure before us, as I say, should be helpful to the export trade. However, there has been one bad weakness on the government's part, and it is this. In dealing with the balance of payments problem, which is so current in these days as indeed it has been for some considerable time, or when that subject is being debated or discussed, it seems to me that the government are looking only at the part that has to do with commodity trade or merchandise trade. Merchandise trade is only part of the problem in the field of balance of payments. The minister again has made grievous mistakes as, for instance, when he liquidated our fleet that was carrying our exports to the West Indies, with the effect of having all those exports that we sent to the West Indies now shipped in the main in foreign bottoms and paid for in foreign exchange rather than in Canadian currency. Losing that earning capacity was a bad mistake. There is also the question of insurance of the ships and other related matters.
Export Credits Insurance Act
Again I mention that matter because this measure must be looked at in its proper context. It appears to be a good measure. We shall wait until we see the bill itself but, as it is worded, the resolution would appear to indicate that it is a good measure with regard to the part of the export trade problem with which it deals. My only hope is that the government, which seems to have made so many and such grievous mistakes with regard to the other larger part of the subject of foreign trade, will follow the example of their actions under this act. In that way we could perhaps really get to the solution of our problems which, I am sure, must weigh heavily on the minds of all hon. members on all sides of the house. I would ask the minister whether he has available for tabling information about the contracts under sections 13, 21 and 21(a) and if he will table it at a convenient opportunity.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Section 14.
Section 14 is the limit of the authority to insure. If that information is available I would appreciate receiving it with a view to doing a bit of questioning on it before the resolution passes.

At the outset I think we should note that we have three pieces of constructive and essential legislation before us to consider today. I think we should remind ourselves that if it had not been for the fact that we have kept parliament sitting against the wishes of those who would try to wreck it in the hope of some quick advantage, these useful pieces of legislation would have been indefinitely held up, to the great inconvenience not only of Her Majesty's loyal subjects but that of the entire Canadian economy as well.
I think this particular piece of legislation is worthy of support, as it enters into one of the basic needs of our economy with regard to facilitating the exportation of our surplus production. The increase that is suggested from $200 million to $400 million, ought to make a worth-while contribution in connection with this entire problem. The only comment I have to make-and I may say I am speaking generally and not specifically-is that the capital for this corporation comes from the consolidated revenue fund. If it is to be increased I think it would be much more practical if it were done through the facilities of the Bank of Canada rather than through the taxpayers' pockets. Why should our internal currency be deflated for a guarantee fund that will be frozen to cover the export situation?
In this regard, I think we have come to a crisis in our problem of international settlements. In the same way that we were in

Export Credits Insurance Act serious trouble internally in the 1930's in regard to the gold standard, so are we now externally in trouble in the 1960's. I believe that serious consideration should be given to this aspect of the problem. I have a number of times suggested that the time has come for us to consider the establishment of a permanent export-import bank that would deal with the problem that is being raised at this particular time through a different approach than the one that is now being taken. But in saying that I am not trying to minimize at all the importance of the point at which this legislation is aimed. I note that there are other amendments of an administrative nature that are being contemplated, but there is very little detail given about those. I trust that they will be made available to us.
In so far as this increase in the assets of the corporation is concerned, and following up the reference the hon. member for Ottawa West has already made, I wonder how much of this money is to be used to finance credits that have been extended to the different communist countries in connection with the sale of wheat. Does this mean that the money will be used to cover past sales, or will it be used for future sales that are contemplated? I think I should make my own stand clear in this regard. It has been confused, perhaps, in the heat of political battle during the election campaign. It is not a question of being against the sale of our surplus wheat to communist countries. It is a question of whether we are fulfilling our obligations to those who are on the friendly side of the fence in this battle of ideologies in which we are engaged today.
In that regard, I wonder what thought the minister has in connection with facilitating the use of these credits about which we are talking to such neighbours as we have in the Caribbean and in Latin America. Certainly with the international threat that confronts us in our own hemisphere at the present time we ought to be giving some lead to this hemisphere in facing up to our responsibilities to the nations that are friendly with us and who are caught in the squeeze that is taking place in the economic struggle so far as the communist ideology is concerned as opposed to the western way of life. This applies specifically right here on our doorstep. It applies, I believe, to the Caribbean right now. It applies to Latin American countries. Following up again some remarks which the hon. member for Ottawa West has made, I believe it applies specifically at this time to the commonwealth as well.
So far as we are concerned, the question involved in whether or not Britain joins the European common group at this time is, what are we going to do in the future if she does?

Perhaps this thing is being precipitated on us faster than we are prepared to meet it. At any rate we still have to face up to it, because Britain in her dilemmna at this time is being forced into some action. I feel, therefore, we should give careful consideration to assuring that a good part of this increased credit is used in connection with commonwealth trade. I believe, too, this could be a starting place with regard to some kind of revision of the settlements problem within the commonwealth of nations. Here we have an organization, which does not need a treaty of Rome to preface it with a political foundation. We have that understanding and that mutual respect for each other that would permit us to go ahead to a greater degree than we already have.
I note also that the minister mentioned the fact this change will permit the government to finance the export of capital goods as well as primary goods. I feel this is essential also and, without going into the details, the general principle is good and deserving of support from every one of us as we are trying to face up to the crisis in which we are at this time.

If it is satisfactory to hon. members I would like to keep fairly current with their questions. I shall not take more than five minutes. The hon. member for Ottawa West asked four questions. First he asked about the operating capital of the corporation under section 14. The operating capital is ten times the aggregate of the subscribed capital and the surplus. The capital is $15 million and the surplus $5 million, making a total of $20 million; therefore the operating limit is $200 million.
Just to clarify that, what about the earned surplus?
It does not give the earned surplus. It is the surplus.
It just says "surplus" in the act.
Any earned surplus is passed back to the Department of Finance.
It does not show that.
The balance sheet does not indicate that.

The hon. member asked me to give him the basis for the 200 million limit,

Export Credits Insurance Act and I am trying to do that. Section 14, page 7, of the Export Credits Insurance Act reads as follows:
The liability of the corporation under the contracts of insurance issued and outstanding shall not at any time exceed a total of ten times the aggregate of the amount of the subscribed capital and the surplus of the corporation.
In section 10 it says the following:
The authorized capital of the corporation is fifteen million dollars, consisting of the five million dollars authorized prior to the coming into force of this section and an additional ten million dollars.
Then over on the next page, in subsection 4 it says:
The amount of five million dollars credited to the capital surplus account of the corporation prior to the coming into force of this section shall continue to be the capital surplus of the corporation.
Therefore it is ten times the $15 million capital plus $5 million capital surplus, making a total of $200 million as the operating limit of the corporation under section 14.
The hon. member also asked what are the outstanding commitments under sections 21 and 21(a). First of all the commitments under section 21, liability under current policies, are as follows: Czechoslovakia, $15.6 million for wheat; Poland, $51 million for wheat; Brazil, $0.3 million for steel rails; Mexico, $10.1 million for steel rails; United States, $61.8 million for aircraft, making a total of $138.8 million.
Then, Mr. Chairman, our additional outstanding commitments at the present time are $34 million for wheat for Poland; under negotiation or other possible wheat sales amount to $21 million, and for possible aircraft sales to $6 million. Therefore we have a total of $138.8 million of existing liabilities and an additional $61 million of commitments giving us a total of $199.8 million out of our $200 million.
The hon. member also asked what business we have done under section 21(a). The business done up to December 31, 1961 is outlined on page 13 of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation's annual report, issued December 31, 1961. In addition to that the corporation has done the following business this year: $1 million worth of road graders, the Dominion Road Machinery Company, passed by order in council 1962-753; General Motors Diesel Limited, locomotives to the amount of $6,048,000 under order in council P.C. 1962-338; and for R.C.A. Victor the item is not specified but I suppose it is electronic equipment, to the amount of $1,620,000 passed by order in council 1962-123. That is the total business done under section 21(a).
The hon. member also asked whether section 21(a) should not be under a separate organization. The answer to that is no. This has

been considered by the corporation, and it is felt there is no reason for putting section 21(a) under a separate organization. The experience of the other two countries mainly concerned with this type of operation is that in the United States their export and import bank handles both insurance and finance, and in the United Kingdom their export credit guarantees department handles both insurance and finance. We see no reason for handling section 21(a) under a separate organization. The operations of insurance and financing are being handled very well by the corporation at the present time, we believe.
The last question the hon. member asked again raised the question of the $50 million wheat deal with China. He asked why it was not handled-
It is $100 million.

The $100 million wheat deal with China. The hon. member asked why that was not handled under section 21. The answer is that in the spring of 1961, when the wheat sales to China were being negotiated by my colleague the Minister of Agriculture, the ceiling of liabilities that Export Credits Insurance Corporation could approve under both sections 21 and 21 (a) was $200 million. The liabilities under policies in force and commitments given totalled $162 million, leaving only $38 million available. As hon. members are aware, the initial wheat sale to China was of the order of $50 million, so it would have been impossible for the Exports Credits Insurance Corporation to insure those sales under the ceiling of liability then in force.
The hon. member inquired whether this extension being asked for now would be used to finance wheat sales in the future, and of course-
Sales to China.

-sales to China, or any wheat sales. The answer is that it would depend upon the circumstances existing at the time and what other outstanding commitments there were. But I would assume that in future wheat sales to any country would be handled by the corporation, provided there was enough money available at the time to handle those sales.
The hon. member for Red Deer made a very constructive and interesting speech. He did not ask any specific questions. I can assure him that the suggestions and ideas he put forward received great attention from myself. I found them very interesting.
My neighbour the hon. member for Dan-forth, who is very close to me, made a very interesting speech also. I listened to it with interest and appreciated the remarks he made

on behalf of his party. I appreciate very much the committee giving me the opportunity to answer questions in this way, and I thank hon. members who, with great consideration, allowed me to keep current with these questions. During the rest of the day I will be looking forward to hearing speeches by other hon. members expressing views on what I consider is a most important measure.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if I may ask a question of the minister and make a very, very brief comment. I noted with interest the minister's remark that in his opinion any wheat sale to China that is made in the near future will be financed through this act if there is money available.
I said, in all probability.

"In all probability" is good enough. I did not want to misquote the minister. The minister outlined some possible future commitments under this act. One item to which he referred was a possible $21 million for the sale of wheat. This is the thing that concerns me in all these statements by the minister. From what he has said there is no indication that China is prepared to take up the balance of the contract soon, because I do not think the $21 million referred to by the minister is anywhere near the amount that would be involved, if this is the case.
I would hope that China will complete the agreement; I would hope this sale can be made soon; I would hope the financial arrangements which are necessary will be made under this act. If it should be that there is not money, then do it under an amendment to the act or by some other means. But it is a bit disturbing to me that the minister has not been able to say this morning that possible sales in the near future would involve much more than $21 million. Therefore I wonder whether he has any information as to the possibility or the likelihood of China going forward with the balance of the agreement and taking up this wheat. There is a tremendous surplus in the country, and farmers are most anxious to have this sale completed.

Mr. Chairman, I would like very much to comply with the hon. member's request and give him the information, but I am afraid I am -not able to do so. That information must be obtained, of course, from my colleague the Minister of Agriculture, under whose jurisdiction the wheat board operates and who handles these wheat deals. My job, through the Export Credits Insurance Corporation is, to handle export credits and export financing when credit and financing
Export Credits Insurance Act are requested; and if they are requested by my colleague the Minister of Agriculture I am very glad to comply. But I am afraid, however much I would like to give the answer, I cannot do so because it must come from my colleague.

Mr. Chairman, I very much appreciate the remarks the minister has now made. I am not endeavouring to be critical of the minister in any way, but it is amazing to me that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not in a position at this time to say that China is likely to take up the balance of the wheat called for in the agreement. I appreciate that it is not in his department; I appreciate that he has to hear from his colleague the Minister of Agriculture. However, I am absolutely amazed that the Minister of Agriculture has not given this information to the Minister of Trade and Commerce or, more specifically, has not been in a position to assure the house and the farmers in the country that this agreement will be completed and the deliveries made in the near future.

Mr. Chairman, I first wish to thank the hon. member for Vancouver South for yielding the floor in order that I might make a brief observation at this time. This is the type of legislation which I think might well be coupled with the greater use of Canadian ports. I was struck by the fact that in his opening remarks the minister said that with which I think we all agree; that is, this measure is good for Canada. I want to suggest that it might perhaps be even better for Canada if it were associated with either regulatory or incentive action to assure that those who benefit from it would spread the benefit by the use of Canadian ports.
The minister, who has a reputation for being sympathetic not only to trade matters but to Canadian ports, particularly in his earlier capacity as minister of transport, well knows that the federal treasury has a very large capital investment in Canadian ports. This is now running to some $368 million, including $39 million at Halifax, $36 million at Saint John, $154 million at Montreal, $40 million at Vancouver and so on; and there are other substantial capital asset investments.
Under this legislation the corporation is empowered to insure certain export contracts and also to finance long term exports of capital goods. I wish at this stage only to ask this question of the minister before the bill passes all stages in the house. Would the minister, in consultation with the corporation, consider the possibility-as other nations do- of coupling this kind of legislation guaranteeing insurability of certain exports and

Export Credits Insurance Act financing promissory paper of other importers with regulatory control to provide that those who benefit from it should utilize Canadian ports throughout in these transactions covered under sections 21 or 21(a)?
If this is not possible within regulatory authority, would the minister consider, in consultation with the corporation, having the corporation make clear to the beneficiaries, including Canadian manufacturers, other producers and the importers, that it is the avowed purpose of the present government where Canadian taxpayer funds are involved, either actually or potentially, that the beneficiaries thereof shall utilize Canadian ports not only for the benefit of those ports but of all those backed up behind the ports-railway workers, highway employees, transport workers and the like.
I would ask the minister to tell us at a later stage in the consideration of this legislation-legislation which I am sure will recommend itself to all members of the house-whether he does not think it would be desirable to insist upon Canadian ports being used under regulatory authority; or, if that should not be possible, whether he does not think it would be wise for the corporation to take all the steps it possibly can to acquaint the beneficiaries of this measure with the fact that since Canadian taxpayers in all parts of Canada are helping to finance this legislation, Canadian ports should have their proper share of the advantages which flow from it.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that the committee is indebted to the minister for having made his additional statement, and for the answers he has given to questions which are raised. I am particularly interested in the development of this corporation because I went back to study the wording when the bill was in resolution stage in 1944. It was then worded in this manner:
Whereas, it is desirable to promote the revival oi trade by establishing a corporation to insure against loss caused by insolvency, delays in connection with the export of Canadian-produced goods, and during the period of transition from war to peace by providing for loans or guarantees to governments of other countries or their agencies-
I think all hon. members in this committee will agree that we have come a long way from the original concept of this corporation. The minister is obviously no longer interested today in the revival of trade. He is no longer a revivalist. I think he is an expansionist today, and I think it is worth paying some attention to the change which has come over the corporation and its concepts.
I have read the annual report for the year ending December 31, 1961, and I would say that it is a statement of a corporation that is exceedingly well managed. I would point out that across the years they have stood behind the sale of over $1 billion of Canadian goods exported to foreign countries, and out of defaults they have incurred a loss of only some $925,000. I believe that is a loss of about one tenth of one per cent, and I am quite certain that any Canadian businessman would like to have his losses out of noncollections reduced to that amount.
I think that a compliment is due to the important and responsible civil servants who are the directors of this organization. In addition, I notice that there is an advisory board. While I do not know personally all the members of the advisory board, I know them by
Export Credits Insurance Act reputation and I may say that they are an exceedingly competent group of Canadians. The only thing that concerns me is that, according to the annual report, it is quite obvious that this advisory board is brought together only once a year. Provision was made for some $2,800 only, I think, for a meeting of the advisory board. I would counsel the minister to give some thought as to whether or not it would be advisable for this advisory board to work more closely with the directors than they have been doing.
The minister suggested that we as members of parliament should be salesmen for the corporation and that we should go back to our people and advise them that these facilities are available. I believe the advisory board are in a better position to do that kind of thing. Two of them are resident in the city of Vancouver and they are very competent people. If those who are interested in using this protection in order to export goods abroad were to get in touch with these members of the advisory board, were to know who they were and were to discuss matters with them, I think it would facilitate many of the representations they make to the corporation itself.
Just before we rose at one o'clock the minister, in reply to the hon. member for Ottawa West, was good enough to give him a breakdown of the responsibilities the corporation has today. This is my only critical comment, and I wish to tell the minister that I am extremely critical with regard to this matter. I refer to the fact that all the eggs are in very few baskets. This certainly was not the original concept of this corporation. It seems to me the concept was to support small manufacturers in Canada. I would hope the minister would admit to us now that he would much prefer to supply backing through this corporation to 10 companies of $100,000 each than to one company of $1 million. Here we have Czechoslovakia with $15.6 million for wheat; Poland with $51 million for wheat; Brazil with $0.3 million for steel rails; Mexico $10.1 million for steel rails; the United States $61.8 million for aircraft; and an additional $34 million for Poland for wheat; possible aircraft sale, $6 million. Then we find the $200 million is gone because the figures total up to $199.8 million. I wish to say to the minister that I would be a very poor salesman for my particular riding as we do not grow very much wheat there. I think one of the weaknesses of corporations such as this one is this. Our government corporations which are doing extremely beneficial jobs seem to have had it impressed upon them that it is almost unthinkable that they do any advertising. I believe the time has come when we should let the public know these services

Export Credits Insurance Act are available by some means or other, certainly by some means that are more effective than those employed at the present time. I would draw that matter to the minister's attention.
I am quite certain that we have in Canada firms which are doing an excellent job in the new field of electronics. Some of them are known already as exporters and do not need the facilities provided by this corporation. However, I think there are many others. Rather than restricting the matter to two or three commodities and to 10 or 12 corporations, I would think we wish the widest possible use of the facilities of the corporation and I think that some advertising in that direction would be beneficial.
My one final concern about this matter is that there might be a tendency-and I wish to put this on the record-or a danger, because of the size of each of these commitments, for corporations to use the facilities of this guarantee as a crutch-and I think the minister needs to be careful in that regard-rather than making arrangements as far as they possibly can, which again was the original concept when the bill was first introduced. There was almost the feeling at that time that we are doing this as a last resort. We would much prefer the corporations to make their own arrangements, but because of political difficulties at the end of the war and, I take it, a tremendous world disturbance in currencies, the government set up this corporation. I think the minister would agree that he would still prefer that as many as possible of the sale arrangements with foreign countries by Canadian corporations be made without the use of this corporation, and that in actuality what he is attempting to do is to make possible sales of Canadian goods in those territories where, without the support of this corporation, they would not be possible. However, I suggest that we should be careful that this facility is not used as a crutch by the larger corporations; and I think there is some indication of that danger in the figures which the minister was good enough to provide to the house before we rose at one o'clock.

May I answer a couple of questions? The hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska asked me whether I could let him know the total amount of losses which the corporation has experienced in its life of 17 years. May I say that the corporation has made payments amounting to $10,613,580 -and I shall be glad to send these figures over to the hon. member-and has made recoveries amounting to $8,515,892, for a net loss on claims of $2,097,688 over the 17 years. As I have told the hon. member and hon.

members, the corporation aims to operate as closely as possible to a break-even point. The net losses on those claims have been covered by the premiums charged on the insurance issued.
The hon. member for Vancouver South mentioned the advisory council and the interdepartmental committee. He asked for some information on the advisory council. May I say that the advisory council met in June of this year and will be meeting again next month. As I think he knows, individual members of the council consult with officers of the corporation, and are consulted by officers of the corporation quite frequently. The interdepartmental committee of deputy ministers and men of that calibre meet as often as necessary to work out policy for the corporation.
With regard to putting too many of our eggs in one basket, as he described it, I should like to clear that point up. I was asked by the hon. member for Ottawa West if I would outline the business that had been done under sections 21 and 21(a), and I did so prior to the luncheon recess. The business done under section 21 is business which is not ordinary, regular day to day business, but that which is decided to be good business by the corporation and is proceeded with for that reason. These are usually large and rather extraordinary sales of wheat, machinery and things of that kind. However, the regular day to day, what might be called bread and butter business of the corporation is done under section 14. A very large number of transactions are carried out under section 14 involving producers of every type, size and kind all over the country. I should be very glad to let the hon. member for Vancouver South have a record of the transactions that have been made. They are very numerous. I can assure him that the corporation has no intention of placing all of its eggs in one basket. We are very anxious to do business with all types of producers in every part of the country. I feel that clears up the point for the hon. member.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The minister has already pointed out the need for an increase in the ceiling on the amount of insurance available, I shall not, therefore, elaborate on that. This need, of course, is due to the greatly increased exports resulting from the government's drive to increase sales abroad. In 1961, Mr. Chairman, exports reached record levels. At the end of July, 1962, exports were 11.3 per cent higher than for the same period in 1961.
Now, as a result of the constantly increasing effort of the government to increase exports, sales abroad will undoubtedly continue

to increase and appropriate financial arrangements must be made to expedite those increased sales. What is the government actually doing to increase sales abroad? I feel, Mr. Chairman, everybody is aware of the fact the government is doing a great deal in this respect. However, I always believe in presenting the facts and I am going to do so for the next few minutes.
The first thing I should like to mention briefly that the government has done to increase sales abroad is the export trades promotion conference held in Ottawa in December, 1960. There were 110 trade commissioners who were brought home from posts abroad for this conference. They met with 1,365 businessmen representing 1,133 Canadian firms for a total of 10,502 half-hour interviews concerning export opportunities. As a result, 1,000 new agencies were established and 860 more are pending.
The second thing I should like to mention is the provincial trade and industrial promotion conference. Twelve of these conferences were held in all ten provinces of Canada between February 1961 and February 1962. There were 4,309 businessmen representing 2,472 Canadian firms who attended. The final conference, I may say, was a completely bilingual meeting in Montreal attended by 1,100 businessmen. I may say that the program was equally divided between exports promotion and domestic problems.
The third thing I should like to mention is trade missions. This is a field of promotion that is concerned with export sales, and is most important. During the period 1961-62 there were 47 missions sent out from Canada. During the period 1962-63 there will be 22 trade missions sent abroad. In the period 196364 it is contemplated that 33 will be sent abroad. I should like to mention the purpose of some of these trade missions. In January, 1962, a clothing mission was sent to Europe. In February, a home heating and associated builders supplies trade mission was sent to Europe. Again, in February of this year, a fisheries products mission was sent to Latin America. There was a forest products mission to the Middle East in March and April. A general trade mission went to Australia and New Zealand in March and April. There was a trade mission to Israel in March and April. An electrical appliances mission was sent to Europe in March and April. A wood products mission went to Britain in April. There was a heavy equipment mission to Latin America last May. An iron ore trade mission was sent to Europe in May. An electrical distribution mission went to Latin America and the West Indies last June. An electronics products mission was sent to Latin America in September.
Export Credits Insurance Act There was a leather and leather products mission to Europe during August and September of this year. A timber mission went to European common market countries last September. I had the privilege of accompanying that mission for part of the time and I will have some comments to make about it. There will be a forest products mission to Latin America in October. An appliances, commercial machines and medical supplies mission will be sent to the Middle East in October, and there will be an organic chemicals mission to Latin America in November. I am mentioning these as concrete examples of what has been done and what is being done to promote our trade abroad. The people say they want facts, and there they are.
Now, another thing Canada has been doing to promote our sales abroad is sample shows. Four of these have now been held this year. Sometimes people refer to these sample shows as fly and buy. These have been held at Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg and Vancouver. Businessmen from the United States are brought over to see the samples of Canadian firms in these cities and to buy them. These shows have been very successful. I should like to mention the one held in Toronto on May 22 and 23 last. There were 122 exhibitors and 123 buyers. There was a show held in Montreal on June 19 and 20 last, at which there were 135 exhibitors and 128 buyers. At the show held recently in Winnipeg on October 2 last, there were 51 manufacturers and 58 buyers. One will be held in Vancouver during this coming week on October 16 and 17. At the moment according to information the department has at its disposal, there will be 46 exhibitors and 64 buyers.
Then, another aspect of the government's efforts to promote sales abroad that has been very successful is trade fairs. I have a list of trade fairs here, Mr. Chairman, at which various Canadian firms have exhibited. The period covered is from January 1962 until March 1 of next year and, of course, some of these fairs have not been held as yet. More than half of them have been held and I should like to mention a few of them. There are approximately 35, but I will mention a few just to give hon. members an example of what is happening.

I mentioned earlier that I had the privilege of accompanying, for a brief period, one of our trade missions to the European economic community. This was the timber trade mission which visited five countries, Belgium, the Netherlands, West Germany, France and Italy. I was only able to accompany it to the Netherlands, West Germany and France, but in view of some of the statements made by the hon. member for Vancouver South last Wednesday I think it might be of interest to the house to give a brief account of what goes on in these trade missions. Apparently some hon. members are quite unaware of what happens.
The trade mission consisted of representatives of 16 business firms, representing the timber trade in Canada. They came from all parts ot the country and from every province. British Columbia, I might add, was mainly represented by MacMillan and Bloedell, Seaboard, two or three other firms and the North British Columbia Lumbermen's Association. The mission visited all centres which had an interest in the timber trade. It visited Rotterdam, Amsterdam, Bremen, Hamburg, Le Havre, Genoa and other comparable cities.
During the daily programs members of the commission had the opportunity of seeing how timber was used in these countries and the type of building construction native to them, so that our salesmen could have an idea of what uses timber is being put to in Europe. They also had an opportunity of discussing timber uses with architects and of showing them types of timber, some of which had previously been unfamiliar to the architects. On other occasions interviews were set up between European buyers and representatives of Canadian companies at which sales of west coast timber, hard plywoods from Quebec, timber from the maritime provinces and Ontario, were discussed. Our people were glad to find out what were the proper European specifications, what type of timber they wanted and how our prices compared with those of other countries.
As I say, I only mention this in passing because a number of people do not seem to be aware of what these missions accomplish.

I realize that the hon. member's remarks last Wednesday dealt with Canadian lumber sales to the United States, but some remarks of his dealt with trade and trade measures generally. For that reason I thought he might find this of interest.
I think he would be interested to know that there is a great reservoir of good will for Canada in Europe, and I would almost be tempted to say that, other things being equal, such as price, quality and the like, Europeans would be more likely to buy from Canada if we have fully comparable products to offer them. Of course if we have better products, then so much the better.
As a result of talks I had with our trade commissioners and other people I found out something I thought to be of great interest. They said that some Canadian products which had been shipped to Europe-I will not mention the trade itself because that might prove embarrassing to some of our manufacturers- were not up to standard. Certainly some of the products that have been shipped to Europe in the past are not quite equal in calibre to similar or identical products from some of our competitors overseas. Some of our products lacked the finish or uniformity of similar or identical products coming from Europe.
I want to pass this information on, and I hope it will get to the appropriate sources in this country. If we hope to continue to increase our export sales-and we have to do this-our manufacturers must realize that European countries and other places in the world are not prepared to accept slipshod workmanship, and articles that are exported must be as good as or better than similar or identical articles from other countries in the world. Most of our manufacturers are doing a wonderful job, but there are one or two instances-and I will not mention the trades concerned-where this has not been the case. I hope those trades will note these remarks.
I could not help observing this when I was over there. Hon. members who sat in the last parliament will recall that we used to hear from time to time in this house remarks by the hon. member for Welland to the effect that nobody in Europe would accept Canadian money. I do not know where in Europe the hon. member was at that time, but in the places I happened to visit, in every hotel and every exchange place the top two currencies on the list were the United States dollar and the Canadian dollar.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to say a few words on this resolution I would first like to convey my congratulations to you in your new position as deputy chairman of committees. I am sure that under your guidance and direction committees will progress with fairness, justice and great expedition.
The resolution which is before us, which deals with two amendments to the Export Credits Insurance Act, is the first piece of legislation that has come before this twenty fifth parliament. I admit that I am very much in accord with what was said by the hon. member for Red Deer, namely that this is one more case when we should put party affiliations aside and get on with the nation's business. This piece of legislation is important to Canada and to the export industries. I am pleased to see this legislation is being piloted through the house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I think it is a just and well earned recognition of his great work on behalf of the export of Canadian products that he should have the honour of piloting the first bill through this new parliament. It must give him a great deal of satisfaction. I know he is regarded throughout this country as Canada's No. 1 salesman. It is through his aggressiveness and his visionary efforts that Canada has achieved her present position in the export field. It was through his efforts last year that we were able to reduce our deficit on international payments to $982 million-the first time for six years it has been below the
Export Credits Insurance Act $1 billion mark. Under the minister's direction, too, we achieved for the first time a surplus of $173 million of exports over commodity imports.
The amendments now proposed to the act deal, first of all, with section 21, which has to do with insurance and, second, with that part of the act which is concerned with export financing. The corporation issues insurance which protects Canadian exporters against non-payment on the part of foreign buyers. It is important to an exporter that he should have protection in this regard. For the interest of the house, the risks that are insured by the corporation are as follows: the insolvency of a foreign buyer, the failure of a buyer to pay to the exporter within 12 months after the due date the gross invoiced value of the goods he has accepted; the blockage of funds, or transfer difficulties which prevent the Canadian exporter receiving payment; war or revolution in the foreign country concerned; and any other cause beyond the control of both the exporter and the buyer arising from events outside Canada, in the continental United States of America, for instance, the cancellation of an export licence, or the imposition of an import restriction on goods not previously subject to licence. This is the type of insurance the corporation provides for exporters. It makes this protection available at no cost to the taxpayer; it is all done on a break-even basis, and it is not available from any private source.
During the past 12 months, the corporation has insured more than $110 million worth of exportable goods covering a very wide range of Canadian products. Incidentally, these products must be of Canadian manufacture to the extent of 80 per cent or more. Such goods have been shipped to more than 90 foreign countries. The corporation has further commitments to Canadian exporters amounting to about $100 million. It is for these reasons, and because of the great increase in Canadian exports-an increase which is averaging about 10 per cent a year-that the committee is being asked to approve an increase in the fund to $400 million.
The amendments to section 21 (a) which the committee is asked to consider involve nothing more than changes of a technical nature. It is a matter of processing the promissory notes in a more efficient way. I am happy to support the two amendments which are before us because I know this legislation is of great assistance to exporters in my own community. I know that the Canadian General Electric Company, which manufactures transformers and sells them to underdeveloped countries, makes considerable use of this service. The countries which import these goods are often

Export Credits Insurance Act not able to pay spot cash for them. Sometimes payment is delayed as long as 10, 15 or 20 years, and it is only by means of the long term finance available through the corporation that the company can make such sales. I can think oi another concern in my constituency, the Guelph Engineering Company, which is making valves and exporting them to Belgium. They, too, are making use of this act and its accommodation. I also think of those who raise purebred livestock in my community. They are exporting livestock to many countries throughout the world and they, too, are making use of the accommodation provided through this corporation.
As I say, I am very much in agreement with these amendments. X shall support them, and I hope every member in this committee will do likewise. Not only do I think hon. members should support this resolution but I suggest they go back to their constituencies and inform those who are engaged in export industries of the wonderful facilities available to them. In closing, may I say I support this resolution so that Canada can continue to make progress in the field of export business, which has been so evident under our direction in the last few years.
