Mr. Chairman, first of all, I should like to join all those who offered congratulations to you on your election as deputy chairman of committees. I also wish to congratulate you on the first remarks you so eloquently made this afternoon. We were certainly happy to hear you say that in your new position, you will follow the rules of fairness and that each one of us will have the opportunity of expressing his views without interference.
(Text):
I should also like to associate myself with those who have expressed the view that we are this afternoon considering changes in the procedure of a corporation which appears to have been very well managed indeed over the years since its inception. Its record both of helpfulness and the exercise of good judgment is apparent from the balance sheet and from the operating statement in the corporation's annual report. I hope that after the proposed increase of the area of its activities the corporation's judgment will continue to be as good as it has been in the past and that it will continue to be as helpful to Canadian exporters and producers.
I listened with interest to the statement made by the minister in introducing his resolution, and felt it was helpful. I did, however, regret his tendency-a tendency of which the hon. member for Ottawa West was somewhat critical-to engage in declamatory statements

of a propaganda type in connection with our foreign trade. Our foreign trade is in a difficult position and we on this side of the house do not feel it will be helped by the making of idle boasts nor by any feelings of complacency.
If I heard the minister correctly, at the outset of his remarks he made the statement that this was a non-profit organization.
Indeed, its object was neither to make a profit for itself nor a profit for the government. This corporation, however, for the past couple of years has, quite rightly under our laws, paid an income tax which is a tax on corporate profits in the amount of about $750,000 a year. Any corporation which pays this amount of income tax is obviously a profit-making organization, and perhaps it is right that it should be making a profit. I do resent, however, any attempt to mislead the people of Canada with the statement that it is non-profit-making.
I was also a little distressed to hear the hon. member for Oxford, in his somewhat tiresome outline of his vacationing in Europe, apparently laying a foundation for the claim that 't was these exercises which had made necessary this increase in insurability or the right to incur additional insurance. One would have been led to believe that these trips had been highly successful and conducted with great success, and that what was needed, following upon these ventures, was to increase the amount of money available and prosperity would be upon us. The same complacency was reflected in the speaker who preceded me, who pointed out that under our distinguished Minister of Trade and Commerce a favourable balance of trade on commodity account has been incurred in 1961 for the first time in a great many years. Unfortunately, this glowing record has been somewhat marred, even though there has been introduced an austerity program accompanied by devaluation of the dollar. I would draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, to the fact that there has been an increase in our exports in the first half of 1962 over the previous year; but at the same time there has been a very substantial increase in our imports over the first half of the previous year. In the first six months of 1962 the favourable balance of trade on commodity account has disappeared, and indeed in the first six months we are faced with a deficit of some $49 million. This is one of the hard facts of life, one of the regrettable circumstances to which we have to face up, and it is a challenge we have to meet. I would suggest that we are not going to be able to meet this challenge by proclaiming to the public that the things which have been done

by the government, and indeed by the business community, have been eminently successful, and that all that is needed is a little more of the same. As a matter of fact, the steps taken have not been successful. We have manifestly not met the challenge, and I suggest that something more imaginative than what we have been getting for the past five years is essential.
I should like to say a word, if I may, directly about the act. As I understood the minister, the resolution contemplated two distinct actions. One was a proposal to raise the amount available for insurance purposes from $200 million to $400 million. I personally would be glad to agree to this, but on the basis that we hope we will be able to find the means to increase our export opportunities by this amount, and not because what the government has already done is going to make this necessary. We have not done enough as a country and mere is roquiieu to be done.
As to the second item, it is a proposal in respect of the long term capital financing to permit the corporation to accept bills and negotiable instruments, including promissory notes, for purchases of our export goods direct from the buyer himself. As I understand the act, this started out as purely an insurance operation; in other words, it was up to the seller, Canadian, and the buyer, foreign to make their own buy and sell operation, to arrange for satisfactory terms of credit and financing, and the Export Credits Insurance Corporation then stepped in merely to guarantee the payment by the buyer. And in its initial stages this was limited to commodity short term credit.
Over the years, as a consequence of amendments made necessary, I suggest, by the changing nature of world economy and trading arrangements entered into by European countries and the United States, it became necessary to give assistance in providing guarantees for longer term operation, but this was still essentially in the nature of an insurance function. But now, if I understand the minister correctly, this corporation is going to assume, to some extent anyhow, a banking function which is quite different from an insurance function. It will be a banking function in that the credit which will be sought by the buyer will be provided by the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, and the debt, the obligation, will be manifested by a note given by the buyer and taken directly by the Export Credits Insurance Corporation. I think this will be a debt which will be the direct responsibility of the government, rather than an obligation secured by the assets of the corporation.
Export Credits Insurance Act
This means, then, that the Export Credits Insurance Corporation will be slipping rather by the back door into one of the major functions of the United States export-import bank. I think a number of Canadian businessmen have for years been urging that this is a function which the government of Canada should fulfil, but I would urge the minister, if my interpretation of the second half of this resolution is correct, to proclaim that we have gone beyond the mere function of insuring credit and are now engaging in a straight government banking operation. My own personal view is that that is a function which, in order to meet international competition,'the people of Canada should have this government perform for them. If we are going to do it, let us be honest about it and not do it under the guise of running exclusively an insurance scheme, as a member of the Berne convention on credit insurance, in a quiet and unobtrusive way, got into a banking operation. I would be glad if the minister would advise me whether I have in fact misinterpreted the object, and indeed the function, of the second part of the resolution.

If I may do so, once again I should like to address myself to some of the questions that have been asked. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo asked me whether I could let him know the amount of insurance that had been asked for by firms in the Atlantic provinces. The answer is that the corporation insures six fish exporters in Canada having an annual volume of $3,440,000. Of those policyholders, four are in the Atlantic provinces and do an annual volume in excess of $3 million. The hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount began his remarks by taking me to task for being, as he said, both boastful and complacent. I should be interested in knowing in what way I was either boastful or complacent. It was certainly not my intention to be either.
Look in the mirror.

I thank the hon. member. That is what I would expect from him. In my opening remarks it was my intention simply to outline what the corporation had done and why it is necessary to do what it proposed. If that was taken as being boastful and complacent, then I am surprised, and I am not convinced that anything I said was either complacent or boastful.
With regard to the question asked by the hon. member concerning the operations of the corporation at cost, may I say that the excess of premium income over expense and valid claims since the corporation started operating 17 years ago is only $1.9 million,

Export Credits Insurance Act after insuring export sales of $1,050 million. Thus the excess is less than one fifth of one per cent which is available to meet losses which might arise under insurance at present in force. I do not think you can operate a business of this magnitude any closer to the line than that.
Then the hon. member spoke about the regrettable position of our exports and imports, that although our exports had been steadily rising year by year, he was very upset over the fact that our imports are in excess of our exports this year and in some way he appeared to blame the government for that fact.
As we all know, imports are made up of the total purchases of 18 million Canadians. If the hon. member or hon. members can suggest any way in which we can cut down our imports without imposing unfair restrictions on our fellow Canadians, I should be interested to hear it. I like to see exports exceed imports.
Why?

Because that situation gives us a favourable trade balance. It puts us in a more favourable international payments position, and that is something that is most desirable in the running of any country.
The hon. member spoke rather disparagingly about the fact that our imports exceed exports this year. May I say that they exceed them by a figure that is about one fifth of the amount that imports exceeded exports in the last year in which the late Liberal government was in power in 1956. I would therefore suggest to hon. members on the other side of the house that, when they criticize the government for having imports in excess of exports, they might look back at the performance in this regard under their own government.
With regard to the government assuming a banking function may I say this. You might call the function that we perform under section 21(a) a banking function. When I took over this portfolio I found in my meetings that I held immediately with the Canadian Chamber of Commerce of which I believe the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount is a prominent member, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and other important bodies there was a universal demand that the government provide long term financing to match what is being done at the present time by other countries. As a result of these suggestions made by these important business bodies in this country this government undertook to extend the operations of section 21(a) to include long term financing for capital goods. I think any businessman in Canada, especially

those who manufacture capital goods, will tell you that this has been of great benefit to them. Many millions of dollars of Canadian business has been done simply because it was possible for Canada to extend the same long term financing facilities to those capital goods manufacturers as are made available to similar manufacturers in the United States, Great Britain, and other countries. It was for this reason that Canada undertook this new function under section 21(a). If that is a banking function, and I suppose it is, I am glad that we undertook it.
The proposed change in the operation of section 21(a) is as a result of requests that we have received from countries to which we have extended credit under that section. These countries would like to deal directly with the Export Credits Insurance Corporation; and it is in order to accommodate them that this slight change is being made. It is not a fundamental change. It is a change of detail whereby the Export Credits Insurance Corporation is allowed to deal directly with the importer instead of dealing with the importer through the exporter. It is simply a means of cutting out one step in the procedure, ui cutting cut red tape; and T think we would all agree that is desirable. When the measure comes before the house I hope that hon. members will agree that is desirable.
I hope I have answered all the hon. members' questions. Once again may I say that I appreciate the courtesy shown by hon. members in allowing me from time to time to rise and answer questions as they are asked.

I wonder whether I might ask the minister a question with regard to rates. It is just a simple question which I am sure the minister can answer. In the annual report at page 5, it is stated that there are approximately $66 million worth of commodities insured at a premium of approximately $1,100,000. This figures out to about 1.6 per cent, the amount of the premium to the amount of the commodities. I was wondering how the rates are calculated for insurance premiums. I was wondering whether or not the rate is calculated having regard to risk with different countries, or whether it is calculated on the basis of different rates with different countries. I should like an explanation, if the minister does not mind.

I am glad to answer that question. On the insurance under section 14 the rates charged vary according to a number of factors, including the country to which the shipment is to be made, the type of goods and in general the risk calculated by the corporation. The premiums average, on the whole, three quarters of one per cent. As 1

say, they vary from country to country according to the risk involved in doing business in a particular country and the chances of receiving payment from importers in a country and the type of goods involved. Each type of transaction is calculated individually and the best possible rate is made available to the individual exporter.
If the hon. member desires some specific information about certain types of products, if he will speak to me afterwards I will make sure he is given the specific information he would like.
I appreciate the minister's offer, but if he does not mind I would rather drop him a line and have him send it to me.

I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce a question relating to the Export Credits Insurance Corporation annual report. The report states that in 1961 pvports to a value of $65,007,223 were insured under this section and the premiums on the 55 policies issued amounted to $1,093,854. This works out, according to my calculation, at $1.66 per hundred. It is certainly not the three quarters of one per cent the minister mentioned.
What page is that?
Page No. 5.
Is that under section 21?
Section 21, yes.

When I said three quarters of one per cent on the average, I meant the average day to day regular business done under section 14. Section 21 would, in all probability, have a higher average premium because it relates to special operations which are over and above what the Export Credits Insurance Corporation believes it is justified in entering into. They are passed to me, as minister, and I take them to the cabinet. If it is decided to go ahead and insure an operation of that kind, it is for a very special reason. They are usually large scale operations with more risk than the average day to day business; but it is considered for one reason or another in the national interest that the corporation should insure these risks. They are in excess of the normal risk and that would be the reason for the higher premium.

May I just ask a supplementary question? I notice that in Hansard for February 18, 1954, the Right Hon. Mr. Howe speaking on this same subject stated that the average premium rate was 82 cents per hundred on all exports covered to date. This is less than 1 per cent of the selling price, and this is under section 21. I wonder,
Export Credits Insurance Act in view of the minister's comments about the risk involved if it means that the risk has deteriorated by approximately 50 per cent?

No, Mr. Chairman, he would be referring to general business under section 14, and other business, whatever that other business would be, would be done under section 21. It all depends on how much business is done under section 21. As I say, if only business under section 14 is considered, I am advised that the average rate is three quarters of one per cent, that is .75 instead of the .82 with which Mr. Howe dealt at that time. The reason for the higher rate about which the hon. member is talking is the business done under section 21, and is the rate of interest that is charged in accordance with the risk considered to exist by the Export Credits Insurance Corporation.

I must, nevertheless, state that I disagree with the views of some hon. members, for instance the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Ouellet) and the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount (Mr. Drury). It is important to discuss this legislation, and to discuss it very seriously, more particularly to see that the public be informed of any action taken in this house to improve Canada's export trade.

Export Credits Insurance Act
This export trade is vital for us because, after all, facts are there to prove that, with a population of 18 million in this country, and a production large enough to supply a people perhaps four times as numerous with primary, secondary and other products, we definitely have to seek the needed markets outside this country if we, in Canada, want to have maximum production, and the full employment that goes with it.
On the morrow of the war, competing nations launched a policy of export credits which enabled them to obtain markets that would normally have been ours. As the years went by, we therefore had to follow in their steps. And, thanks to certain efforts, we sometimes overtook them.
Today, in the world as we know it, it is impossible to do any business with foreign countries without offering to the possible buyer the terms of sale and payment which will meet competition. And it is the reason why we have to show some imagination and devise legislation to improve the situation like the one now before the house.
Thanks to this measure our manufacturers will be able to finance their sales on foreign markets. Our manufacturers and merchants will then be able to make sales which they could not even consider without this amendment now before the house.
If I take the floor today, it is for two reasons. First, because I think the people are not sufficiently aware of the benefits provided by this measure concerning export credits insurance.
I think it would be wise to ask hon. members, each time the occasion arises, as well as newspaper men, to point out to our population, by all means at their disposal, that there are very useful export credit facilities for those who wish to increase their business.
A moment ago, the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount, whom I am happy-with certain reservations-to see here in this house, blamed the Minister of Trade and Commerce for being, to use his own words, declamatory about what has been done in the field of trade and industry, about what he is now doing, and about what he intends to achieve.
I believe it is somewhat daring to blame the minister for being proud of what he has accomplished for, after all, thanks to his efforts to promote our export trade and to the measures he has introduced in this house since he has assumed the direction of the Department of Trade and Commerce, the volume of our exports has increased sharply. In fact, according to figures which are already six months old, our exports to the common market countries have increased by


more than 16 per cent, while the increase is more than 90 per cent to eastern Europe, 36 per cent to Latin America and more than 35 per cent to the Asiatic countries.
These figures surely indicate that under the direction of the minister, the Department of Trade and Commerce has obtained results which are very beneficial to the whole population and to the Canadian economy in general.
The important thing that we have to deal with is surely the promotion of the development of the Canadian economy in all fields, and I believe that it would be hard indeed to find, in this house or elsewhere, people who will deny that increased sales will result in an increased industrial productivity, which will mean more employment for our citizens, more benefits for the industry, the employer and the employee, and, consequently, more benefits for the state, benefits which will be distributed for the greatest welfare of the Canadian community.
Mr. Chairman, may I repeat that, according to my way of thinking, the main objective of all our economical activities at present is to look for the appropriate cure to remedy the depressed situation of the economy, where it is to be found, so as to overcome this dreadful plague of unemployment, which is unfortunately striking certain parts of our country.
The main task of the members of this house is to see to it that, with the rising of the level of business, we can also adequately raise the level of our economy so as to secure full employment and the prosperity hoped for.
Mr. Chairman, I believe that the resolution now before us, even if it receives general support, must be presented by all our advertising media as one of the essential measures for the future of our economy. It is because this question is so important that I have taken part in this debate.
Several approaches can be used to improve the state of our economy. Some advocate methods which might bring about inflationary pressures. Others see the solution of all our problems in the full nationalization of industry. And, it must be pointed out, certain citizens see-and wrongly so-in socialism or in semi-socialism the cure for all evils.
I, for one, believe that in a country as young as ours, with such a bright future ahead, socialism is but an approach of premature senility. In my opinion, before venturing to apply economic theories not yet proven nor established, we must take good care not to

bring about in this country an inflation which might have here the same disastrous results as those we have noted where socialism has become a form of government.
What is certain, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that, thanks to this amendment, everyone will benefit from an increased business flow, and thanks to this measure now before the house, I am convinced that all manufacturers and merchants will now have the opportunity of increasing their business. And this is in keeping with our desire to work for the welfare of the Canadian community.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I did not hear the interjection of the hon. member, but I am leading up to what I hope will eventually come under this act. I am sure, also, that the contacts made by the representatives of the Ontario flue cured tobacco growers marketing board while they were abroad will be very helpful in promoting future sales of tobacco. It is quite feasible and possible that tobacco sales to prospective purchasers in European countries will need financing, and I hope the committee will give favourable consideration to the early passing of this legislation in order to make available the additional amount of money required by the corporation.
I was very interested to hear the minister this morning suggest that all hon. members of parliament take advantage of the functions of this corporation. I have found the president, Mr. Aitken, to be very co-operative in providing information to myself along these lines. By making this information available to all hon. members I think we will be put in a more favourable position to pass along to our own local industries some of the benefits and advantages provided by this crown corporation.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a word or two with respect to the bill before the committee. I think we must be grateful to the hon. member for St-Antoine-Westmount, for indicating what really is a fact, that the function of this legislation has changed over a period of time, and latterly from primarily an insurance function to a banking function. I think I am correct-and


if I am not, I would ask the minister to correct me-in saying that as late as the last amendment, what really happened was that a Canadian seller and a foreign buyer got together, made a deal, and through the facilities of the banking system somewhere obtained credit. The note which became the evidence of this transaction was then delivered, through the banking system, to the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, and in that fashion the sale was guaranteed. Through this new approach by the government we have actually direct access by a seller to the Export Credits Insurance Corporation. We can avoid, therefore, the transaction through the banking system.
I am sure that we on this side of the chamber are heartily in favour of anything that is going to step up our export industry; I think we are all agreed on that. We are indebted to the minister in a number of ways. I think every hon. member on this side of the chamber recognizes that he has been a most aggressive salesman. Another thing we appreciate from the minister is the fact that when matters are raised in this house and in public, quite frequently he is factual and honest with us to an extent that breeds confidence in these matters, which frankness we do not always enjoy from every member on the treasury benches. Even going back to the Ghana episode, there were many instances when we felt the minister was prepared to bare facts to us. In this fashion perhaps we in this committee of minorities can be more co-operative with respect to measures such as the one before us which are designed to develop and improve the economic situation of Canada.
I believe I am correct in saying that under the GATT negotiations of 1947 as amended, if commodities are subsidized in export by any of the GATT signatories there is provision for the country importing those goods to impose dumping duties. I think we have to be honest enough with ourselves to recognize what is the kind of transaction we are now performing. We had a little word of advice and counsel from the Associate Minister of National Defence a moment ago, telling us of the advantages of private enterprise and how this was something that would stimulate investment. Actually what we are doing, it would appear, is publicly subsidizing finance in this particular instance. Let us face that. Collectively the Canadian people are doing something here in the credit line, as well as the insurance line, that apparently has not been done in the past.
We are concerned when we hear suggestions that these $200 million, this 100 per cent increase, is now necessary because we are simply expanding so well. The hon. member

Export Credits Insurance Act
for St. Antoine-Westmount a few minutes ago alluded to the trade deficit in the first six months of the year, the current problem. I do not think we on this side are particularly worried about an immediate problem if the long term solutions seem to indicate progress. But a number of thoughtful people are rather concerned about this six months period because it appears to be indicative of other problems. "The Industry", published by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, refers to the past six months as being actually our Achilles heel. Indeed, in some respects one might question whether or not the austerity program is really designed to meet the immediate and short term problem demonstrated by this Achilles heel of the past six months.
We on this side want to face these trade problems honestly and bravely but one of our difficulties is that we do not have ready access to a lot of relevant facts-facts, for example, relating to the exchange rate, the balance ox trade, and so on-which are important if we are to be constructive and co-operative. We are disturbed by evidence which is reaching us from other sources such as the National Institute Economic Review. This periodical, which is one of the principal authorities on this subject in Britain, indicates that Canada has dropped from first to eighth among the nations of the world in per capita foreign trade and from fourth place to fifth place in absolute volume of trade with other countries. According to the same publication, in all but two years, 1953 and 1954, in the long administration of the Liberals Canada stood first among the nations of the world in per capita foreign trade. By 1960, Canada had declined to eighth place behind even Trinidad and New Zealand. In absolute volume of trade with other countries, Canada had been fourth for many years. In 1960, Canada had slipped back to fifth place.
Along with these facts we read that Canada's living standard has dropped from second to third place. I do not wish to depart unduly from the subject under discussion, but I interrupted the minister a moment ago- and I apologize for having done so-to ask him why he considered it important to have what is called a favourable balance in trade. It seems to me that most economists agree it is a desirable thing to have a balance- a long term balance is what we are interested in, not a short term balance; we are prepared to accept that within short cyclical periods there may be adverse balances which, in the long run, produce development and growth. We are concerned, however, with these other factors which are completely relevant to the problem we are dealing with at the present time. We do not believe that you can ignore the important operations which are taking
place in other parts of the world in the common market area, in Latin America and in the United States. However brilliant the minister may be as a salesman or as a promoter he can never be successful if the over-all policy of our country is such as to ignore these larger developments. It has been suggested that we are simply dragging along as a tail to United States policy-that we show no evidence of what this country is prepared to do should Britain, for example, join the common market-as we think is desirable- or, in the contrary situation, should Britain decide to remain outside.
It seems to us that these are the more profound issues which lie behind this question of Canadian trade. While we are anxious to expedite the passage of any legislation designed to improve matters, we believe we should face the fact that for some years the Canadian trade picture has nut been heaitny. We recognize that profound changes have taken place in the world since the sellers market which followed the war. The former Liberal administration, we realize, cannot take all the credit for the situation which existed during that period and, similarly, the present government finds itself faced with far reaching changes which are bound to affect the world trade pattern. On the other hand, we question whether these profoundly important events have found a suitable response in the policies of the present government. I am sure that for our part we shall be agreeable and co-operative with regard to this measure, but there is one reservation I should like to make. We do not want this corporation to be used for nationalistic tactics, like the tariff surcharges which was another nationalistic tactic. To do so would ultimately weaken our position in an expanding trade community. This is one of the reasons we are concerned about the exchange problem. This, again, could be considered as a nationalistic tactic which is out of step with the times and with the great opportunities presented to us, particularly by the situation now developing in Great Britain with respect to the common market.

I thank the hon. member for Leeds for his thoughtful remarks. I should like to answer two questions which he raised. First, he was worried that consequent upon our amendments to this act we would in some way be bypassing the banking system. I should like to assure him that in the longterm financing arrangements we would not be avoiding or bypassing the banking system. The corporation will pay the exporter by cheque through the banking system, and will ultimately receive payment from the foreign buyer through the banking system.

Export Credits Insurance Act There is no intention to bypass the banking system in any way, and the proposed amendment dealing with section 21(a) is simply a minor amendment designed to facilitate our doing business with a number of countries which have requested that we do business with them more directly.
We also have no intention of using the Export Credits Insurance Corporation as a nationalistic tactic, to use the phrase which I believe the hon. member used. The whole function of this corporation is to provide a service which has been found during the past 12 years to be in the interests of Canadian exporters whether they be industrialists, miners, fishermen, producers of primary products or manufacturers. They need this insurance and they need this export financing. In all the other major industrial countries of the world such facilities have been provided in roughly the same way. In the United States, for instance, there is the export-import bank and in Britain there is a similar type of corporation. The Canadian government operated to provide the facilities for our producers both in insurance and in long term financing. Again, I wish to thank the hon. member for the very thoughtful presentation of his views and I am glad to be able to assure him on those two matters about which he was concerned.

I have a question which I should like to put to the minister, but before doing so I may say that I doubt whether there is any member of this house who would not give full support to a measure which would increase the ceiling or limit on the amount of guarantees to Canadian exporters in order to enable them to increase their exports to the countries with which they trade. In this connection I am sure the minister will recall that one of the first communications he received after he was appointed Minister of Trade and Commerce came from myself. In it I outlined the tremendous advantages both to the exporting country and to the importing country of such institutions as the export-import bank in the United States, and the corresponding German agency. I expressed hope at that time that there would be a similar development here. Now, admittedly two years later, a move is being made in the right direction.
My question arises out of the second part of the resolution. The minister said, I believe, that it was intended to provide for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act. If I followed the minister's remarks this morning correctly, these changes have to do with machinery which would make it possible for the government to accept bills of exchange and other negotiable paper,


including promissory notes, from the buyer rather than from the exporter. The question which concerns me is this: would the government be discounting the bills of exchange? If not, what is the point of getting a bill of exchange?

The purpose of this amendment is to do simply this. At the present time, when a deal is being consummated between an exporter and an importer, the importer agrees to pay the exporter by a series of notes, which the exporter endorses over to the Export Credits Insurance Corporation. The corporation then holds the notes, receives payment from the importer, and by arrangement, pays the exporter on certain dates for the goods, the machinery, or whatever it may be, that he is exporting. This amendment is designed to allow the importer to deal directly with the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, and saves the necessity of the exporter bringing the notes to the Export Credits Insurance Corporation and endorsing them over to the corporation.
That is just one step which is eliminated. It will also allow the Export Credits Insurance Corporation to sell the note, the instrument, which it has received from the importer, and to sell that instrument or any part of it to any buyer who finds that kind of instrument attractive. The purpose of that is that then there is not so much drain on the $300 million which is available to the corporation for doing this kind of long term financing. This amendment will also allow the Export Credits Insurance Corporation to make a loan to the buyer of the instrument, if the buyer of the instrument wishes to obtain a temporary loan on that security from the Export Credits Insurance Corporation. This will enable the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, in its opinion, to do its business more easily. That is the purpose of the amendment.

That, Mr. Chairman, is the thing that is bothering me. That would indicate that the Export Credits Insurance Corporation is going into the banking business, if it is going to sell bills of exchange to third parties. That is an extraordinary development in credit insurance. Is that not more properly the function of an export-import bank?

Well, Mr. Chairman, the operation which the Export Credits Insurance Corporation carries out under section 21(a) was literally forced upon it by the unwillingness of Canadian banks to perform this function for our exporters. For many years, I understand, there have been conversations with the banking community on behalf of our exporters suggesting to the banking community that they undertake this role of providing long term financing for our exporters. But the

Export Credits Insurance Act
banks in Canada were unwilling to perform this function, and so, if the function was to be performed, it became necessary for the government to perform it through the Export Credits Insurance Corporation. There was no desire on the part of the government or the corporation to get into this business. It was literally forced into it to provide a necessary service to our exporters. The chartered banks formed an export corporation-I am sure the hon. member is familiar with that operation-which provided financing for medium term business; that is up to five years but not more. So the Export Credits Insurance Corporation has been forced into a banking operation, which it had no real desire to get into, because of the need to provide this financing service for our exporters. But being in that kind of financing operation, through no choice of its own, it now desires to do the job as efficiently and as well as it can. That is the reason for these changes.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in this debate, but would the committee bear with me if first I expressed my personal appreciation and the appreciation of the people of Edmonton for the honour done our city by hon. members of this house in choosing my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton West, as its Speaker. I am sure that Mr. Speaker has already added to the honour done our city by the way he has handled his job. I know I speak for the hon. member for Edmonton East as well as myself, and in fact for all residents of the Edmonton area, when I wish him well, and we hope that his tenure of office will be long, successful and happy.
In this debate, Mr. Chairman, I have been following just about all the speakers with considerable attention. I realize that the subject can wander quite widely, dealing as it does with financing trade around the world.
I am sure that an hon. member can quite readily discuss every aspect of government policy in connection with exports on the ground that only by looking at all other efforts closely can we determine whether the government really needs this amount of money for which it is now asking in order to assist this method of helping finance our exports and increasing those exports.
The hon. member for Ottawa West made some remarks about the changing position of trade patterns and the changing problems since the war which I thought deserved to be dealt with a little more fully, and which I thought, considering the method by which he handled them, should be answered somewhat sharply. I noticed that the hon. member's speech on this matter merely said that he did not like the way we handled these problems,
but was entirely devoid of any constructive suggestion as to how we could have handled our trading problems better. In fact he was devoid of any specific criticism as to in what area we have made an error. I am sure that if the hon. member looks at his speech tomorrow in Hansard, he is going to find that it amounts to no more nor less than sour grapes.
I think that what is required if we are to add anything to this debate, and if we are to justify to the country the granting of this money to the government, is that we should take at least some look at what the changing trade patterns have been, and at what have been the changes in trade problems. I was happy to hear the parliamentary secretary to the minister give us a run-down on some of the things this government has been doing to meet these problems. I am sure most members of the committee are aware that since the war we have seen revived and renewed industries in such countries as Germany, Italy and Japan, who have, with the latest machinery and techniques, with new methods of financing, and in fact with some help from former enemy countries, hit traditional markets with an impact never felt before. We have had to face that in good part as Canadian businessmen with some worn out machinery. We have had to see new and severe competition in established markets, and in fact have had to absorb this loss at home. But the fact that Canada's export trade is in the position it is now is certainly some indication of the success of this government's efforts in meeting the new trade problems and patterns. One of the new problems that directly bear on this subject I believe is the new method of trading and securing trade from other countries. It is no secret to members of this house, I am sure, that the government of Japan, for instance promotes-I was going to use the word "permits" but I think "promotes" would be the better way of putting it-trade cartels, that it actually assists in the merger of large well financed and well organized companies in order to form cartels for the purpose of most effectively moving into overseas markets. Other countries have such trading organizations and many countries have schemes somewhat similar to ours in order to assist the exporters in financing their sales whereby either the government insures or finances them and in many cases goes further and finances a new industry in order to move into these new markets.
I therefore say that any suggestion that this government has not faced new problems or the changes in the problems can only come from members who have not taken the trouble or who have not had the capacity to

Export Credits Insurance Act understand the vast change that has taken place in government handling of these trade patterns in the last few years.
I am sure that every businessman in Canada who is exporting or hopes to export has looked with considerable interest on the trade conferences called. From the attendance at those conferences and the spirit with which businessmen have entered into them, it is obvious that these conferences are most helpful. Trade missions to other countries have been singularly successful. I am personally acquainted with many people who have gone on them and who are now doing business selling products in South America, Central America and other parts of the world, something they have conceded to me would never have come about were it not for the action of this government.
In short, Mr. Chairman, I think what hon. members opposite have failed to observe really is that there is an entirely new concept of government and that this new concept was designed because of the changing pattern and changing problems of today's more complex world. It is no longer enough for any government or any political party to sit back and to say that ours is merely the task of creating an atmosphere in which private enterprise can flourish. With today's trade problems that is not enough. The government itself is obliged to take a more active part, as it has been doing, in making sure that the trade problems around the world are more thoroughly investigated by their trade officers.
The government itself has found it necessary to find new ways in which to pass along information to our own Canadian business. It has had to find out more details about the trade problems and the financing problems of the other countries and to maintain, through such things as the new design council, the productivity council and so on, new methods of getting the required information back to our manufacturers who, under a private enterprise system, really must carry the ball and make these sales.
The suggestion that we are going into banking is one that I have been struggling with for a long time. While we may not like to see the government acting as a banker, the fact is that in today's fierce competition, in our need for expanding markets we are obliged to use whatever methods are necessary to achieve that objective. Today's trading patterns have another complexion in that traditionally Canada has been a supplier of raw materials. However, especially since the advent of automation we have found that being a great supplier of raw materials is not the best way in which to provide the steady, well paid jobs to which the people of

this country are entitled. In the last few years we have been trying to become more and more a manufacturing nation. This attempt, of course, has required a great amount of financing. It also requires an intensified search for markets at a time of increasing competition. I do not think we need to say any more than that in justification of the government's acting as a sort of banker, if that step is necessary.
I myself have had occasion to urge on the government something a little further than that, by reference to what happened in just one South American country recently. I was approached by a very large businessman in Canada who told me about a project recently undertaken by an Italian company, whereby the Italian company obtained a turnkey contract for the whole job of drilling a couple of hundred oil wells, I think it was, putting together the pipe line system and building the refinery to handle it, and turning over the key as a completed project to the government. I understand that the government that was getting this work done-and the total cost was approximately $196 million- was going to pay for it over a period of 10 years. We in Canada have facilities to do all that. We have the businessmen with the technical know-how, the mechanical skill and the personnel to be able to handle a project of that size. The gentleman who approached me was quite willing to organize it, to put it together and to go out and sell it. However, I do not know of any businessman we have who can take on a project of that size, namely, one of approximately $196 million, which could be completed in two years when he would have to wait for the payout over a ten year period.
My suggestion then to the government on this matter is that the further sum for which we are now asked may prove to be inadequate and that the act as it now reads may not be flexible enough. Perhaps there should be a little more leeway for the government so that, instead of handling so many small projects, they will also be able to handle a project of approximately $50 million or $100 million without going into a panic.
I am aware that, with changing conditions, some of these markets in some South American countries may be a little bit risky in some respects. As we know, there is much unrest in some of these countries. We know that, even where there is not much unrest, the financial situation of the country itself may not lead to too much confidence. All of these factors certainly must be taken into consideration. Wherever they are factors I suggest that the government, through its trade commissioners and external affairs offices, has the facilities which will enable

them to determine to a much greater extent than can the Canadian industrialist, just how important these factors are. I think these sources of information and government assistance, not only in determining the risk but with all other market factors, have been invaluable. I believe that sometimes the best way in which to make sure that the government is giving the best service along this line to the industrialist is for the government to have a small financial stake in there as well.
I thought I should comment on just one more remark made by the hon. member for Ottawa West who said he did not like the handling of the Cuban trade system. When I asked him to comment on what his stand was, he merely said that we should not annoy our good friends the Americans. I wish that he could have been a little more helpful in answering my question.
when it is in order, I will.

I am afraid that during the question periods in the house and during the last campaign, every comment on that situation by hon. members opposite has been in the same vein, "Do not annoy the Americans." There is never any suggestion about Canadian interests, never any suggestion about what they would do differently as compared with the policy of this government. I would suggest to hon. members opposite that they should have a little more regard for our own country and a little less regard for the possibility of stepping on the toes of our large friend to the south. After all they are powerful friends, but also very understanding, with a system of government about the same as ours. They appreciate frankness, and I am sure it does not help much to be continually saying, "Do not annoy our American friends".

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a suggestion to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, particularly in view of the signing of the Kennedy trade extension act of yesterday. Since the government has decided to go into the banking business, I suggest we change the name from the Export Credits Insurance Corporation to the export bank and insurance corporation.

As most hon. members who have spoken before me have suggested, Mr. Chairman, there seems to be general agreement in all quarters of the house in favour of the principle of this measure that is before us. Personally, I should like to express appreciation to the minister for his lucid presentation of the legislation. As my own colleagues who spoke earlier have suggested, we in this section of the house are particularly gratified 27507-3-31
British North America Act with the success of this corporation's efforts, indicating as they do, the virtue of efficient planning and public enterprise business.
The one concern I have on reviewing the success of our trade efforts as expressed here today, has to do with the large volume of that success which is apparently tied to the export of Canadian wheat to China. My colleagues and I are in agreement with this trade; in fact, we have urged for many years that it be started. When we review the facts of the case, I am a little concerned myself at seeing how much of the success of our recent trade efforts has been geared to these sales to China. I feel we should realize that had it not been for three successive typhoons which destroyed part of the wheat crop in China, the Chinese would not have been buying wheat from us. Had they not been buying wheat from us, our trade picture would have been much poorer than it is. It would be facetious to suggest to the minister, but not without point, that he investigate the prospects for typhoons in China in 1963. Again, I should like to compliment the minister on his presentation.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Hees thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-63, to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-9, to amend the British North America Act 1962 (redistribution) .
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a very simple bill. I brought it before the house in each session of the last parliament, and while we had some interesting debates it never received approval, was never sent to a committee or given any great examination. The purpose of the bill is set out in the explanatory notes, as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to introduce in subsection (1) of section 51 of the B.N.A. Act, 1867 the underlined words "independent of the Parliament of Canada," so that the readjustment of the representation in the Commons be done in future by an independent body rather than by a committee of the House of Commons.
In going through my notes, Mr. Speaker, I found this from the Ottawa Citizen of March

British North America Act 7, 1959. The heading is, "See Federal Election
May or June of 1962". The article reads, in part:
Douglas Fisher (CCF-Port Arthur) said Friday in the Commons he has "a pretty good hunch" that the next general federal election will be in late May or early June, 1962.
He based his prediction on the belief that if Prime Minister Diefenbaker calls the election for a later date he will be faced with a redistribution of the 265 seats in the Commons.
My prediction was on the mark and this parliament, of all parliaments, Mr. Speaker, considering its makeup, is faced with the question of redistribution. In view of what is expressed in the speech from the throne I can only assume that the government intends to proceed in this matter. However I would hope it would not proceed with the bill that was brought before us at the end of the last session, when parliament was just dissolving, the electoral boundaries commission bill.
I know that many of the new members in the house are not aware of all the complications, difficulties and problems related to redistribution, but yet the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Walker), new as he may be but being aware of the problems of his constituency, must realize that his constituents are a perfect example of the failure of what is just basic democratic justice, that is, representation by population or equal strength of votes.
Without going into too great detail in relation to this, I would like to offer to new members of the house a paper which I prepared some time ago listing all the areas, in square miles, of the various constituencies in Canada, their populations in the census of 1951 and 1956, their estimated populations in 1957, and I hope very shortly to have it brought up to date covering the 1961 population figures.
Basically our constituencies are supposed to be determined by their population. That principle is inherent ever since confederation, although it has been badly marred in its operation. The principle is that the vote of each Canadian should be equal one to the other. Let me give this example at the present time in rough terms, because it is the most apparent one. I do not want to comment on the reasons for the disparity, but a voter in Scarborough needs 19 people voting with him to have the effect of one single voter in Iles-de-la-Madeleine.
Let me put it another way and stay within a single province. The vote of the voter who put the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) into this house, was diffused five times from the vote that brought the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) into


the house. An example with less disparity is that the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Badanai) sits in this house with a factor of not quite half of the hon. member for Port Arthur, whatever party he may represent, because the population of Port Arthur is that much larger.
In our constitutional arrangements under the British North America Act with regard to determining constituencies, the requirement is that after every census each ten years, a redistribution takes place to take into consideration the changes in populations; but through a number of adjustments that have been made, Canadian politicians-and I do not think this is any disgrace on their part-have compromised and compromised away the equal vote principle over the years.
I can give some examples. There is a population of approximately 100,000 on Prince Edward Island at the present time and there is a population of almost 300,000 in a constituency such as Mercier in Montreal and York-Scarborough in Toronto; yet Prince Edward Island has four seats. Other examples of such populous constituencies are York Centre, Carleton, one Edmonton constituency as well as a couple in Vancouver, each of which is represented by only one member.
The reason in this particular example is that there is a so-called Senate floor written into section 51 of the British North America Act, which provides that no province can have less representation than the number of senators it has. At the present time two provinces, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, have this Senate floor. This is fine. As provinces, this guarantees them representation in this house that cannot go any lower; but what is happening to a province such as Saskatchewan? We have a 15 per cent escape clause written into section 51 as a result of the activities of the Right Hon. James Gardiner and other politicians of that province. They did not want to face up to the number of seats Saskatchewan was going to lose after the 1951 census, so they put in an escape clause which, if it remains in for the next redistribution, will save Nova Scotia from losing one seat, as well as Saskatchewan, although it cannot serve Saskatchewan so well as it did last time.
Saskatchewan and Manitoba, still above the protection of the Senate floor, are being reduced more comparatively than the provinces that have already reached the Senate floor; and because we have a ceiling on the number of seats in this house, namely 265, provinces such as Ontario, Alberta and Quebec, whose populations have grown faster, are not given the requisite number of seats

in any adjustment, that in terms of equity might come from Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.
This is a very complicated situation, and all I can argue from the record, from the past statements of the Prime Minister, is that the application of change in this situation should be dealt with by an independent commission. That is the reason why I have brought this bill forward. It seeks to amend the British North America Act and underlines the point that we should have a redistribution commission independent of parliament.
In order to make my case for the bill I can do no better than refer to Bill No. C-87, which was introduced late, towards the end of last session, and which I hope all new hon. members will study. It was a bill entitled:
An act respecting the establishment of an electoral boundary commission for the readjustment of representation in the House of Commons.
There are many criticisms we can make of that bill, but there was no opportunity to make them during the last session. Instead of setting up a commission that is independent, that bill proposed setting up a commission that would report to parliament, or lay its report before the Speaker. There was no requirement in it that its report should be acted upon at any time, and I want all hon. members to look at some of the escape clauses in that bill which would in effect ruin any impartiality the commission might have.
In saying that I am not talking about the impartiality of the people who might compose the commission. I am talking about the escape clauses that exist in the bill, and in clause 12 of it there is this final escape clause:
notwithstanding anything in rules (a), (b) and (c) -
-which set out the rules under which the commission could operate-
-where, for any reason, the commission is of the opinion that the strict application of those rules in any particular case is not practicable or would be likely to produce an inequitable result, the commission may make such departure therefrom as appears to it to be practicable or to be necessary in order to avoid that result-
That is nothing but a blank cheque. I do not know what it is a blank cheque for, but the whole intention surrounding this commission was that it was to be an ad hoc one. That is, it was to be set up for this occasion, and the only permanent man named on it was to be the chief electoral officer.
Can hon. members imagine the devil of a position the chief electoral officer would be in if he were to be the only permanent member? The other members could send in the report and they would leave the chief 27507-3-31i
British North America Act electoral officer to answer for it. In passing I may mention that two of the other members were to be judges, and some of us have doubts about the complete impartiality of judges.
It is not my intention to tear the electoral boundaries commission bill apart, but I do want to give forewarning to hon. members that in some ways this cannot be a partisan issue. I would like new members to look at that bill and see what the government proposed. I would like them at the same time to examine the bill I now present, and I ask for their support because I think my bill would force or require that any legislation the government introduces on this matter would be a better bill, a more impartial bill, than the one they presented in the last parliament.
There is to my mind a real urgency here, and I address this urgency to my friends of the Social Credit party. At the present time it is apparent that this government stands sustained in this parliament as long as it has the voting support of Social Credit. I put it upon the conscience of Social Credit members, not in any flamboyant way as did the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) when she was needling them the other night, but just from this point of view. If they are going to sustain this government for long enough, say 18 months or two years, I would like them to begin to think that we must have redistribution and we must proceed with it; because as every month and every year goes by the injustices, the inequities of our present situation continue. If they do not give cooperation in seeing that we get redistribution at the same time as they support the government, it is quite possible that we will almost reach the next redistribution before the Canadian people are represented as they should be, and as our law really requires.
Mr. Speaker, I would hope that, because this bill is so simple and because the principle it supports is so apparent and so logical, it would not find any difficulty in receiving second reading and being sent to the committee of this house that has sat on a number of occasions in special circumstances with regard to electoral measures.
I think now is the time for us to have a germane discussion on this whole problem of redistribution. I can say to my Liberal friends, despite all their intense desire to get out on the hustings and get to the electorate, is there not a case made out, before we have such a test, that the Canadian people should have their rights of voting adjusted?
I have one last point, Mr. Speaker. In the United States this whole issue has reached tremendous proportions in the last 18 months. Malapportionment is what they call it in the

British North America Act United States. Some American individuals, zealous of their rights as Americans, took it to the courts. They took to the courts the fact that their vote was not worth as much as some of the rural votes, the fact that the United States congress is dominated by rural representation because of this malapportionment, and they won a verdict that has resulted, both in the states and in the whole federal apparatus, in an adjustment towards giving a decent break on this question of one man, one vote-on an equal basis.
I have tried to find, personally, a lawyer in Canada who can provide me or some of my friends with an injunction or an order of some kind-under the bill of rights, if you would-that would allow us, or me, or one of my friends to bring some kind of an action to prevent, if necessary, an election until the injustice of our present constituency representation system is corrected. So far it has been beyond the ingenuity, perhaps the brainpower, of my friends. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate may have richer sources to draw on. In any case, I feel there is a real issue here, both in abstract and practically.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to explain to hon. members why I have been interested in this question. I represent a riding that is almost one third of the land area of Ontario. It has a population splattered all over the place. It is a most difficult riding to represent well, in the sense of keeping in touch with your constituents. I tried to find out why this disproportion of a high population plus a huge area had been allowed to develop. I was told that at the times when redistribution did come up, the Liberals would get together in their little Ontario caucuses and say, "What sort of adjustments are you fellows looking for?" And they always found that the previous member for Port Arthur, the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, really was too busy to take any interest. As a consequence Port Arthur remained the same, while all around constituencies were being adjusted.
One of the consequences of this partisan approach and the disinterest of Mr. Howe has left an anomalous situation that the New Democratic party representatives inherited. My hon. friend from Timmins has a lovely little pocket borough, as I call it, 35 miles by 35 miles, that he can jaunt around in an afternoon; and he has a population just about half of what Port Arthur has-and Port Arthur is 500 miles north to south, 365 miles east to west.
I am not complaining about this situation, but I would like the house to understand the kind of disparity that has resulted from our practices in the past. I think the onus to


really reform now is most important, not because I think an adjustment in favour of the urban voter is going to bring any great advantage to my party or to any other party, but I think it is a matter of increasing importance in the interests of this country that relate to the urban dweller. So many of our problems today are becoming increasingly related to metropolitan areas, large cities, suburban areas, to housing, planning, welfare and things like that; and at the present time- make no mistake about it-in almost every part of Canada those areas are underrepresented and the favour has gone to the rural and the traditional areas.
I can count on other hon. members in this debate pointing out some of the striking changes that are in prospect in Quebec and some of the other provinces. British Columbia, to an extent, and Manitoba in particular have given the federal government a lead in a sense, since they have put the apportionment of the constituencies on a fair basis. I would hope that-

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Port Arthur asks us to consider his bill favourably, partly on the basis that it is very simple and because its principle is apparent. It is for the very reasons that it is simple and its principle is apparent that I oppose it.
There is a resolution on the order paper dealing with the question of an electoral boundaries commission, to be reintroduced by the government this session, which appeals to me despite the strictures of a similar piece of legislation which the hon. member mentioned. It appeals to me because it does not include the very thing that I find objectionable in the hon. member's bill, and that is the operative phrase "independent of the parliament of Canada".
If we are going to pass a bill of this kind, if we are going to say that it is more desirable in Canada to do the business of Canadians and of parliament through commissions independent of parliament, then let us all pack up and go home, because if we are incapable of this function, we are capable of no function. It is time we started to think in those terms.
Granted, there have been, I have no doubt, abuses in the past. If you deal only in the past, if you deal only with the methods and considerations of the past, I suppose you can find a basis for a bill of this kind. But surely

it would be far better to find a method of dealing with this problem by which parliament retains its rights, by which parliament retains its responsibilities, before we pass a piece of legislation that takes it out of the hands of parliament and makes the whole subject independent of parliament. Parliament would never be able to regain its position, if that were done.
I am not one of those people now-perhaps five years ago I was-who believes that the solution of all our problems and the correction of some of the anomalies that exist in the government of the people of Canada at any level can be achieved by independent commissions which the politicians cannot touch. After all, whom do the people come to for their representation? They come to the politician. They do not expect to find the politician's hands so completely bound that he cannot act on their behalf when they bring him their legitimate problems. Over and over again it is becoming the case in Canada that when people come to see their elected representative, he cannot do anything on their behalf because he is confronted by a board or a commission or a tribunal of some kind, independent of parliament.
I am surprised to find that the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) has introduced a bill with these words in it, because I seem to recall that in times past he has dwelt at some length in this house on the erosion of the responsibilities of parliament. He has suggested on occasions in the past that we are becoming limited in our ability to act because the executive has taken away from parliament the powers of parliament. Do not these boards, commissions, tribunals and such also take away the prerogatives of parliament, giving them to people whom we cannot even reach through correspondence, or even in party caucus? I believe the suggestion that we could solve this problem by taking the ultimate responsibility out of the hands of parliament is no solution. It would only create another problem.
The suggestion that a commission of technical experts might make recommendations to parliament is in my view far more satisfactory because if those recommendations were based on a careful and impartial assessment of the electoral pattern it would be a very difficult thing, or a very foolish thing for a government to reject the findings of such a commission. I have no doubt that any such findings would receive careful scrutiny in the press and elsewhere. The people would be fully aware of them and if they appeared sound, were properly presented and logical in their reasoning it would be a very brave parliament or a very foolish government which would endeavour to upset them. Before
British North America Act changes of this magnitude are made I believe we must try to establish a procedure more satisfactory than the procedure of the past, but not as sweeping as the proposal put forward by the hon. member who, apparently, contrary to so many professions of principle he has made in the past, is now prepared to say to us: admit you are incompetent and dump the job on another board. That, I am not prepared to do and therefore I cannot support a bill such as this.

I had always regarded the hon. member for Port Arthur as a sort of grass roots egghead. I must say therefore that I was astonished to discover yesterday-and I cannot congratulate him on this-that the hon. gentleman has now joined the Prime Minister in that witch hunt for bureaucrats. I must say the performance of the hon. member was perhaps a little more literate than that of the right hon. gentleman, but the principle was the same.
It is very odd to find the two of them in the same boat, and all the odder when one thinks that the hon. member is the grass roots branch of a party which more than any other party has prided itself on being composed almost exclusively of intellectuals, highbrows and academics. This may be the new element in the New Democratic party. However, having joined in the witch hunt for bureaucrats last night, the hon. gentleman today comes in to suggest the creation of super-bureaucrats, as the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke has just pointed out, who would be independent of everybody-even, presumably, of the Supreme Court of Canada.
I read the bill this morning when I heard it was coming up this afternoon and I can hardly conceive of anyone in this house seriously thinking that parliament could so abdicate its functions as to suggest that a responsibility which the constitution gave to parliament in the first place should be handed

British North America Act over in a final way to someone else without any power of review. I must say I found myself in agreement with a good deal of what was said by the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke about the desirability of having a non-partisan commission do the preliminary work and make a report. Indeed, I would go even further, perhaps, than the hon. gentleman would go. I would impose on such a commission the duty not merely of making a report but of drafting a bill of a kind that they thought would, in a non-partisan and equitable way, redistribute the representation in this house. I would make it an obligation upon the Speaker to lay that bill before this house, and upon some officer of the house to introduce the bill into the house.

Notwithstanding what the hon. member for Port Arthur has said about the desirability of one man's vote equalling the vote of another, we cannot lose sight of the fact that this country is a federation of provinces, and that such a federation would never have been made in the first place if it had not been understood in those regions which in some respects are less favoured by geography, and in certain other ways, that they would have additional weight in the parliament of Canada to counterbalance to some degree their geographical and other disadvantages. But it seems to me that in his intervention he provided another powerful argument against his bill. An independent commission is not going to be independent, it seems to me, if it is going to be bound by all sorts of rules and regulations. I for my part would be far more interested in an amendment to the British North America Act which would correct any anomalies that any hon. member feels there are now in the fundamental law. In that respect, sir, I think that when we do come to consider the setting up of a nonpartisan commission which will report to parliament-I am not seeking to anticipate a future debate in saying this-it is very important that we should prescribe the broad rules under which that commission is to operate. We should not give them, as the hon. member for Port Arthur described it in his speech, a blank cheque, but we should tell them what the rules are to be, for example, what the maximum population for any riding should be. I think the hon. member made a real case there. It really is a scandal to have ridings as large as Scarborough and some of the others which have been mentioned. It is even more scandalous to have a riding such as that represented by my indefatigable friend from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador which contains about four fifths of the area of the province of Newfoundland and has a larger population than any other constituency in the province. That is an anomaly. It is an anomaly which now exists only because the government neglected its proper duty to redistribute before the last election. There are, of course, a good many other anomalies of that sort.
Another thing said by the hon. member for Port Arthur with which I agree is that it would be very desirable, if it can be accomplished, to have the redistribution take place before there is another election. I say "if it can be accomplished", it would be very desirable. In fact, under the constitution it could have been done before the last election. Before the last election the government had over 200

members in this house, they could have carried out their constitutional responsibilities had they wanted to, and it is rather unfortunate that this matter has been delayed as long as it has. However, I would not favour -and here I disagree profoundly with the hon. member for Port Arthur-putting any more impediments into the constitution in the way of inflexible rules which will prevent the people from exercising their will, however imperfectly they are able to exercise it because of the distribution of seats in this house, whenever that is necessary in the public interest-and it may very well be, almost any day, sir, as Your Honour well knows, because of the composition of this house.
So I would not want to see anything done which would freeze this particular house or this particular parliament for any length of time. However, I think that because it is a constitutional obligation, this is a matter in which the government should not delay. I think this particular piece of legislation should be brought forward by the government at once; that it should be given priority over everything excepting really urgent financial questions till it is dealt with; and that the commission should be set up equally without delay and urged to report with all possible speed. Because it is the duty of every hon. member of this house to uphold the constitution and to uphold what is, after all, as I think the hon. member for Port Arthur very rightly said, in a fundamental way the basic provision of the constitution, and that is that the people shall be fairly represented in this house which purports to speak for the people of Canada.
As to the desirability of having the basic work done for the redistribution by a commission, I do not think there is much disagreement in the house any more. I do not think there was in the last parliament, and I hope there will not be in this one. I did not understand the hon. member for Okan-agan-Revelstoke to object at all to having a non-partisan commission. I listened to him carefully, and I am sure I understood him to say that he favoured it. But he insisted that its report should come back here to be dealt with finally, in this house and in the other place, before it became law. That is precisely the position, of course, which is taken by my hon. friends in the official opposition. I do not know whether the hon. member for Port Arthur is speaking for the New Democratic party through this bill, which would take the final disposition of the matter out of parliament altogether, but I had always thought previously that that was also the position of the New Democratic party.
