In any case, I do not think that anyone any longer wants to have a committee of this house do the preliminary work of redistribution. I think there is general agreement that this should be done by persons who are less partisan than we are here, and by persons who will be as non-partisan as can be found in the country. Here I would like to say that I hope we can find such people without making too great a demand upon the law courts, because whatever is done is going to displease a lot of people and there is going to be a real danger of imputing motives to those who do it, and of dragging judges into politics, which I have never favoured myself. It seems to me that there are other nonpartisan persons in this country who could be drawn upon to compose such a commission without calling upon the law courts.
There is just one final point. I think that when a commission comes to be set up it should be set up by parliament and its membership settled in parliament. It should not be left to the governor in council to appoint the commissioners. Because surely the last thing we want to do, under the guise of getting a non-partisan commission, is to switch the redistribution from this house to the governor in council. That is what we would be doing if we accepted a bill which gave to the governor in council even the formal power to appoint the commissioners. They should be named in the legislation itself.

However, there are a number of questions that would have to be answered before we would consider ourselves to be free to support the measure presented. However,

Mr. Speaker, I was glad a while ago to hear the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) express, in his usual unassuming way and with some humour, the rather socialist ideas which are typical of the New Democratic party.

The member for Port Arthur told us that the constituency he represents had an area of 300 miles by 500 miles, that is to say, almost of the same size as France. Even if the area he represents is as large as the territory General de Gaulle looks after, its importance is somewhat different.
Be that as it may, I believe that a redistribution of the electoral districts of Canada will become absolutely necessary. But how should it be done? I am inclined to agree with the person sitting next to me, the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Fleming), who feels that a commission should be set up to define the boundaries of the districts to be represented in the forthcoming parliaments. I am of the opinion that a commission should be appointed to study the technical aspects of redistribution and report to a parliamentary committee which would examine the situation and decide upon the changes to be made.
I realize that French Canadians do not always show the utmost respect for parliamentary rule. For my part, I believe that such a procedure would show the greatest consideration for each province and, consequently, for the people of the different areas of Canada.
When my friend the hon. member for Port Arthur refers to unequal representation in such ridings as Scarborough, Iles-de-la-Made-leine, Mercier and Vaudreuil-Soulanges, he speaks of entirely different situations. Thus, when he mentions representation according to population, he means that each citizen is to be put on an equal footing, that is to say, that the voters should be divided into equal numbers. That is absolutely wrong. Indeed, he claims that we are all equal. Well, I suggest that the only time we are equal is when we are born and when we die. Throughout our life, in everything that happens, in everything we do, we see that we are not equal.
I do not mean by this that one area of the population is not equal to another, that one individual is superior to another. We are all equal with respect to taxation and, therefore, with respect to representation in parliament. Apart from that, we are not equal.
It would not be logical to compare a riding of 50,000 or 60,000 voters in a large city with a rural riding of 12,000 or 20,000 voters.
We must realize that city people have identical problems, while rural people have different ones. For instance, you have on the one hand the worker living in a city who is only a tenant and whose sole interest is to increase his salary in order to provide for the welfare of his family while on the other hand, you have the farmer who owns many acres

of land and a herd, who has a responsibility, not only towards himself, but towards the whole community and who must all year round keep an eye on all developments and on measures introduced by the government in the public interest.
If I draw a parallel between those two citizens, I submit that when voting time comes around, the farmer will be able to make a more objective decision and show less partisanship than the city dweller who has never been concerned with administrative matters or been involved in election work.
Besides, that is proved by the fact that when an election is called, there is always a great number of city people who do not vote. Why? Because it is not in their interests to voice an opinion or still because they do not know for whom or for what to vote. On the other hand, one finds very seldom in rural ridings an elector who does not hold decided views or change opinions when some party offers certain advantages or advocates a policy more beneficial to rural citizens.
It is not my intention to draw a parallel between city people and farmers, but rather to indicate that certain rural citizens are interested in politics, in general, compared to those living in cities.
An example of this is to be found in the influence exerted by Canada. Actually, our country, with a population of only 18 million inhabitants approximately, exerts a much greater influence at the United Nations and within international organizations than some nations of Africa or South America which have much larger populations. Why is that? Simply because our country is entirely civilized, because our cities and towns are well organized and our citizens are in a better position to express pertinent views about the current situation than certain citizens of those less privileged countries with a lower level of education.
This shows undoubtedly that representation should not be proportionate to the number of electors, but should be established rather according to the various regions, the different racial, cultural and industrial groups, and in ratio to the number of people with more interest and education than the others.
Consideration will also have to be given to representation by province. In my opinion, certain provinces do not have the representation they should have. I feel it is most im-27507-3-32

We must recognize the fact that each of the ten provinces has different characteristics, different problems and is self-governing. Consequently, each province must have proportional representation if Canadian unity is to be maintained.
I am sure all our Liberal friends in the opposition will join with us in that regard. Even if we do not quite agree with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pick-ersgill)-

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING ADJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
In rising to speak on this measure, Mr. Speaker, I find myself in complete agreement with my colleague, the hon. member for Okanagan-Revel-stoke. When I first looked at the bill I noticed the underlined phrase, "independent of the parliament of Canada". I am very much against that principle. It seems that now we are continually confronted with boards and commissions which are independent of parliament, independent of a member, and so on. I have always been against that idea, and particularly in so far as it relates to a question such as this.
It may be well and good to talk about one vote being equal to another vote. However, we must have representation by the people and we must have representation for each segment of the country, for each industry in the country. What would happen if this principle of one vote equal to another were adopted? What would happen if this idea were projected 20 years from now, with the drift towards urban living? We would have hardly one seat in this house which was truly representative of agriculture. The control of parliament would be in the hands of the large urban centres. There would hardly be a seat in this house which would be dependent upon agriculture, and agriculture would not have its proper representation, as a result of the economic importance we must place on this industry today.

British North America Act
This question of redistribution has come up from time to time federally, just as it has come up in every province of this country. While I do not agree with the government of Alberta very often, I find myself in agreement with them on this question. The government of Alberta considered redistribution within the last couple of years, and they took into consideration the importance of the different industries in that province, the different segments of the province, along with the principle that one vote should be equal to another vote. It is all right to say that we should have an independent board. I gathered from the hon. member for Port Arthur that he wanted this to be a permanent body. What would it do in between each ten-year period? Certainly it would be an inflexible body. It would go on for years and years studying this same question. It would be very difficult to reach and very difficult to change. Certainly, in my opinion, this board would not be as good as the commission that could be set up under the resolution that is now on the order paper.
This commission would report to parliament, and would give parliament an opportunity to have a voice on the question of redistribution, to make sure that there was representation for the various industries. Certainly, when the census is taken every ten years we can see the continual shift of the population. I could give figures which would indicate that perhaps 10 per cent of the population depends upon agriculture for its living. Certainly these remarks could be related to other industries such as the coal industry in the maritimes, the oil and gas industries and so on. I feel quite strongly that all these industries need representation.
The hon. member for Port Arthur also indicates that he accepts the permanent floor placed under representation in the B.N.A. Act. He accepts it with regard to Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. He, therefore, accepts a deviation from his principle which he has outlined of one vote equal to another. I think we must go further than this initial deviation which he has already accepted, and we must accept the fact that industries of prime importance to this country must have representation in this house. This representation must be a continuing thing. We should not be able to look ahead 10 or 20 years and see this representation dwindling away so that ultimately important segments of the country will have no
voice in the development of this country. After all, Mr. Speaker, we are sent here to govern, to regulate the economy and to develop this country. Without representation from the various segments in the country, without representation from the different industries in the country, this would be a very difficult job to do.
May I call it six o'clock?

speechtext:
We will start on Monday, Mr. Speaker, with the bill founded on the resolution which was passed today in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce dealing with the Export Credits Insurance Act, and take second reading. The second item will be the resolution standing in the name of the Minister of Agriculture dealing with the Farm Credit Act which is No. 16 on today's order paper. The third item will be second reading of Bill No. C-3 in the name of the Minister of National Health and Welfare dealing with food and drugs, and the fourth item, the resolution in the name of the Prime Minister dealing with the electoral boundaries commission, which is No. 14 on today's order paper.
I imagine this will take us the most of Monday and Tuesday. The order of business I have announced will hold except for the fact that I want to consult with one of my colleagues. If there is a change in the first two items, I will let the members of other parties know by noon on Monday.

speechtext: May I bring to the attention of the house leader the fact that the Minister of Finance indicated the estimates would be tabled on Tuesday. I take it there has been no change in that, and I presume we will have an opportunity of discussing them during the course of the week.
